One KU Facilities & Other Resources Boilerplate Library

The One KU Facilities & Other Resources Boilerplate Library is a resource that supports proposal writing and development by providing boilerplate text for the University's many facilities and resources. The library is crowd-sourced, gathered and vetted by numerous contributors. The content will evolve over time with new and updated information as it is made available.

To use this library, first select the items you want to export to Word. Click on a section header to expand it and see all the available text. Clicking the checkbox in a section header selects all sections below it. Alternatively, you can pick and choose the individual subsections you want to use. Once you are done, click the "Export Selected Sections" button below, which will generate and download a Word document for you to use.

This content will be continually updated; therefore, we recommend you refer back to this page to access the most up to date versions of sections.

Each entry has been written and reviewed by the content owners. If you have questions specific to the entry, contact the individual(s) listed as the point(s) of contact. These POCs receive an annual reminder in January to review and edit their content as needed. If you identify information that is incorrect, out of date or missing, please reach out to the Research Development Department.

Campus & Institutional Descriptions
►
The University of Kansas | v2026.10 | Point(s) of Contact: Karen Dietz

The University of Kansas (KU) is a Carnegie R1 institution of higher education with more than 31,000 students over five campuses: Lawrence, Overland Park, Kansas City, Wichita, and Salina. KU offers more than 400 degree and certificate programs and has nearly 40 major research centers and institutes supported by more than 40 core research labs. Recent rankings place 55 of KU's academic programs in the top 50 among public universities. As the state's flagship university, KU hosts the sole medical and pharmacy schools in Kansas. It also operates one of only two law schools in the state.

KU's research excellence is reflected in its membership in the Association of American Universities. KU research and development expenditures climbed to a record $610.6 million in fiscal year 2025, surpassing the previous record of $546.1 million by 12% and marking a full decade of sustained research growth. KU's research enterprise is deeply connected to the university's service mission, generating employment and research-related spending and activity across Kansas. KU supports researchers in moving discoveries from the laboratory to practical application through commercialization, licensing, and startup development activities when appropriate. In 2025, KU researchers disclosed 85 inventions, and the U.S. Patent & Trademark Office granted KU 31 utility patents.

►
The University of Kansas Medical Center | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Emily Miller

The University of Kansas is a leading public research university that delivers comprehensive research and teaching programs via its expansive, multi-campus structure. This multi-campus system is comprised of the University of Kansas Campus in Lawrence; the University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC), with campuses in Kansas City, Wichita and Salina; and the University of Kansas Edwards Campus in Overland Park. Founded in 1905, KUMC spans 50 acres within metropolitan Kansas City, KS and includes extensive research and clinical facilities. KUMC has the ultimate objective of improving lives and communities in Kansas and beyond through partnership and innovation in education, research and health care. KUMC is home to the schools of Health Professions, Medicine and Nursing. More than 3,800 students are enrolled every year in KUMC’s 50+ academic programs. KUMC’s Kansas City campus shares a physical location with The University of Kansas Hospital, which provides clinical care for patients and serves as a primary clinical training site for our students. Together, we are a world-class academic medical center and destination for complex care and diagnosis.

The scientific environment at KUMC fosters success in researchers. In FY2024, federally funded research spending totaled approximately $138 million, having more than doubled total federal research spending since 2017. The robust and growing KUMC research infrastructure includes an NCI-designated Comprehensive Cancer Center, an NCATS-funded Clinical and Translational Science Institute, and one of only 35 total NIA Alzheimer’s Disease Research Centers nationally.

►
The University of Kansas Lawrence Campus | v2026.10 | Point(s) of Contact: Karen Dietz

The main campus of the University of Kansas (KU) is in Lawrence and hosts the bulk of the undergraduate programs as well as 13 of the 16 schools that comprise the university. Many courses for the more than 400 degree and certificate programs are taught in Lawrence classrooms. More than 25 core labs, six libraries, four museums, and a multitude of other scholarly spaces support students, faculty, and staff who conduct research in applied sciences, arts, humanities, and natural, life, and social sciences.

Contributing to KU's strengths in security, energy, and health research, more than 15 major research centers and institutes on the Lawrence campus facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration and align discoveries with local, national, and global needs. These research centers include two state surveys — the Kansas Geological Survey and the Kansas Biological Survey & Center for Ecological Research — that maintain datasets and produce scientific reports that support natural resource management, water conservation, and ecological preservation. KU Innovation Park, located adjacent to the Lawrence campus, complements KU's research enterprise by providing technology incubator facilities, laboratory and office space, entrepreneurial support services, and industry connections that strengthen pathways for research translation, entrepreneurship, and commercialization.

►
The University of Kansas Edwards Campus | v2026.10 | Point(s) of Contact: Karen Dietz

The University of Kansas (KU) Edwards Campus is a 34.8-acre branch location that offers more than 80 undergraduate and graduate degree and certificate programs for adult learners, transfer students, and working professionals in the Greater Kansas City metropolitan area via late afternoon, evening, and hybrid online/on-campus formats. The Edwards Campus serves more than 2,500 students, more than one-third of whom have children high school age or younger. Around a quarter of Edwards Campus students are the first in their families to attend college, reflecting the campus's role in expanding access to higher education and workforce development opportunities for regional residents.

The Edwards Campus is part of the Johnson County Education Research Triangle (JCERT), a partnership among Johnson County, KU, and Kansas State University that supports research facilities and educational opportunities intended to strengthen the regional economy and quality of life. The partnership includes the KU Clinical Research Center in Fairway, Kansas, and facilities on the Edwards Campus such as the BEST Building, which houses programs in business, engineering, science, and technology.

KUMC Centers & Institutes
►
Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (ADRC) |  v2025.09 |  Point(s) of Contact:  Ashley Baker, Jennifer Freund

The University of Kansas Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center (KU ADRC) supports and promotes brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) research. This P30-supported center is one of 35 National Institute of Aging-designated ADRCs. NIA P30 designation was awarded in 2011 and renewed in 2016 and 2021 with Russell Swerdlow, MD serving as the Center Director and Jeffery Burns, MD serving as co-Director. In FY24, the KU ADRC accounted for 25% of all NIH dollars coming to KUMC and 16% of all NIH dollars coming to the Lawrence campus. The KU ADRC supports organizational, regional, national, and international investigator-initiated studies and over 100 investigators. Center infrastructure is provided through well-defined cores that include an Administrative Core; Clinical Core; Data Management and Statistics Core; Neuropathology Core; Outreach, Recruitment, and Engagement Core; Research Education Component; Neuroimaging and Neurovascular Assessment Core, and Biomarker Core. Internationally recognized strengths of the Center include its research programs in mitochondria and brain energy metabolism, lifestyle modification for AD prevention, and biomarker development.

►
Administrative Core

The KU ADRC Administrative Core oversees operational and strategic planning. Over multiple cycles of P30 support, the Core managed robust growth as the KU ADRC transitioned to become a recognized leader in AD research with strengths in mitochondria/metabolism, lifestyle intervention, and prevention research. In addition to defining Center strategy, the Administrative Core manages the resources needed to support its investigators. This includes biospecimen procurement plans; consent and compliance requirements; ensuring biospecimen storage; and facilitating access to biospecimens, data, consultation, and other Center services. The Administrative Core advises the other KU ADRC cores, monitors their productivity, and promotes their cooperation. It verifies NIA programmatic obligations are met and maintains Internal and External Advisory Committees (IAC; EAC). It developed and now leads a pilot project program in which ~2/3’s of recipients receive external grant support. It works with junior and senior local investigators to develop successful AD research programs and initiate external recruitments to fill faculty gaps.

In addition to anticipating and managing day-to-day operations, the Administrative Core responds to unanticipated opportunities. Examples include hosting a KU ADRC “site visit” at a national ADRC meeting, an NIA Director’s Regional Conference, and multiple visits from the State’s senate and congressional representatives.

A critical function of the Administrative Core is to ensure all KU ADRC components receive adequate financial resources. It accomplishes this by identifying and procuring dollars from organizational ADRC stakeholders, strategically disbursing funds, and submitting P30 supplements. The Administrative Core promotes progress towards multiple stated goals of the National Alzheimer’s Project Act and advances the main National Plan to Address AD Research Implementation Milestone focus areas.

Specific duties of the Administrative Core include: budget development and oversight; monitoring core activity, resource utilization, and compliance related activities; coordinating and supporting EAC, IAC, and progress report activities; managing the Center’s Developmental Projects Program; pursuing faculty growth and expansion; promoting existing program growth and new program development; adapting and creating infrastructure to match intellectual needs; optimizing the use of existing resources and procuring new resources; managing public relations, government interactions, and national NIA/ADRC activities and priorities; and planning and guiding strategic growth.

►
Clinical Core

The Clinical Core of the KU ADRC is a cornerstone for research on Alzheimer's disease and related conditions. Key features of the Clinical Core include:

  • Cohort Recruitment and Maintenance: The Core follows over 450 participants annually, including approximately 200 individuals without dementia (nondemented) and 200 with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) or AD. These participants undergo standardized evaluations as part of the National Institute on Aging’s Uniform Data Set (UDS).
  • Participant Engagement: Cohort members are characterized and maintained for longitudinal studies, facilitating cross-sectional and longitudinal research.
  • Recruitment into Studies: The Core assists investigators in recruiting participants for investigator-initiated studies, offering access to a well-characterized cohort. This recruitment mechanism enables the evaluation of experimental interventions, including diet-related studies targeting brain health and function.
  • Collaborations with Memory Clinics: The Clinical Core works in tandem with the Memory Care Clinic at KUMC, a regional referral center for memory disorders with approximately 4,000 patient visits annually.

Integration with KU Resources: The KU ADRC Clinical Core operates closely with the Frontiers Clinical and Translational Science Institute (CTSI) and the Hoglund Biomedical Imaging Center (HBIC), ensuring access to state-of-the-art facilities for imaging, data management, and clinical trials. The integration extends to laboratory resources located at the Hemenway Life Sciences Innovation Center and the Higuchi Biosciences Center, enabling comprehensive biochemical and metabolic investigations.

Team Expertise: The Clinical Core is supported by a multidisciplinary team comprising psychometricians, research assistants, coordinators, senior scientists, postdoctoral fellows, and administrative personnel. The leadership, under the direction of Dr. Jeffrey Burns, is augmented by nine clinicians specializing in dementia and AD. This expertise supports advanced investigations, including studies on the impact of dietary patterns on neurodegeneration and cognitive decline.

The infrastructure and resource-rich environment make the KU ADRC Clinical Core an exemplary platform for research into dietary interventions aimed at enhancing brain health in aging and AD populations.

►
Data Management & Statistical Core

The KU ADRC Data Management and Statistics (DMS) Core is directed by Jonathan Mahnken, PhD and is comprised of faculty and staff from the Department of Biostatistics & Data Science. Areas of faculty expertise includes medical informatics, observational data analysis, clinical trials, brain imaging data analysis, power and sample size calculations, Bayesian data analysis, adaptive trial design, survival analysis, and mixed models. A top priority of the Department of Biostatistics is to provide collaborative support for biomedical research across our institution.

DMS Core computers that are connected to a 10 Megabit per second local area network that provides more than 36 Gigabytes of network file storage. Networked file servers provide constant hardware backups of stored data through mirrored storage systems and daily tape backups are also performed. Weekly tape backups are stored off site for additional protection of research data. The network is managed by a Certified Network Engineer who provides installation, training, and maintenance on all information systems. The Department of Biostatistics local area network is connected to a switched, 100-Megabit Ethernet backbone that provides high speed Internet access through the KUMC Internet-2 communication network. Currently KUMC’s Internet access is via a DS-3 (45 Megabits per second) connection. This high-speed network provides each workstation with access to the World Wide Web, electronic mail, electronic file transfer, and shared CD-ROM-based databases.

The Core maintains a statistical analysis server with 24 Xeon CPU cores at 2.4 GHz with 64 GB of memory, 4.2 TB of available hard drive space, a D2D4004 dynamic de-duplication backup device, and an LTO-4 Ultrium 1760 tape backup system; a shared high speed workstation with dual Xeon 3.6 GHz processors, 4 GB of SDRAM, over 800GB of high speed storage, digital tape backup, and a DVD read/write drive; three Dell 2.8 GHz computers with 40 GB hard drives and 1GB RAM; one Dell 2.4 GHz Xeon with 120 GH hard drive and 1 GB RDRAM; two Dell 2.4 GHz computers with 40 GB hard drives and 512 MB RAM; two Dell Pentium 2 GHz laptops with 100GB hard drive.

►
Neuropathology Core

The neuropathology lab is set to provide high-quality and efficient service outlined in this proposal including pathologic diagnosis. The physical laboratory space is optimal in size with standard lab equipment, safety provisions, and modern equipment to conduct experiments. Dr. Haeri’s lab, when combined with a shared space exclusive to his use, has a total of 784 ft² dedicated to the service described in this application. Both the main lab (Lied G003, 594 ft²) and a shared equipment room (Lied G008, 190 ft²) have sink(s) and a chemical fume hood. Lied G003 is the main lab for histology equipped with standard machines to process, embed, and cut the tissue in preparing glass slides for immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence stains on paraffin and frozen tissue sections. The lab is also equipped with both bright field and fluorescent microscopes and onsite ADC glass slide and paraffin block storage systems. Lied G003 has a bay dedicated for brain grossing, processing, freezing (using liquid nitrogen or plates), and photography for documentation.

►
Outreach, Recruitment & Engagement Core

The KU ADRC is the premier dementia research center, and the only NIA-designated ADRC serving the population of the southern “Central Plains.” The KU ADRC Outreach, Recruitment, and Engagement (ORE) Core is an award-winning centralized team and infrastructure that links investigators, providers, agencies, and the public in the region offering a range of resources and education to support research program development and participant recruitment.

The KU ADRC ORE Core has established the necessary engagement and recruitment infrastructure for the proposed project. The Core boasts a mature operation with a scalable team of full-time staff, including an Operations Director, Community Engagement and Recruitment Coordinators, Marketing Coordinator, and several intake specialists. This centralized recruitment model has annually enrolled more than 500 people per year since 2020. We have published on our centralized recruitment model infrastructure, the Participant Relations and Outreach Manager for Trials (Vidoni, 2018, Alzheimer’s & Dementia), a research registry and relationship management database of several thousand active research volunteers. Our charge back model for investigators is rooted in evidence and real-world costs (Vidoni, 2020, Contemporary Clinical Trails).

Building Research Interest and Trustworthiness through Service

The Core uses a “Service First” model to build community interest in research participation (Vidoni, 2024, A&D: TRCI). Our model recognizes that our relationship with the community is not forged through research participation, but mutual support rooted in community-identified needs, regular community advisory and “town hall” meetings”. To this end, the ORE Core has built a service infrastructure as a feeder for research recruitment.

  • Education: The ORE Core provides education under the MyAlliance brand, including in-person and online platforms, and regular Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias (ADRD) best practice education programs for healthcare providers.
    • Over 100 annual events.
    • Webinars, and talks reaching ~1,800 unique individuals annually, providing them with valuable information on dementia research and care.
    • MyAlliance newsletter and events reach several thousand people weekly.
  • Dementia Care Support: The KU ADRC Cognitive Care Network, closely aligned with the ORE Core, provides comprehensive care management, through social work and support groups.
    • Provided training to ~100 providers, including those serving rural areas.
    • Provides care management to ~1300 families annually, including 9 rural counties.
    • Caregiver support texting program (CuidaTEXT/CareTEXT) available in both Spanish and English.

Reflecting Our Region

The KU ADRC is in Greater Kansas City, a bi-state area with a population of 2.2 million people. The metropolitan area includes 15% of older adults identifying as other than non-Hispanic/Latino White. In the five core counties alone, the over-55 population is 581,000, with 99,000 (17.5%) identifying with a minoritized community. The region encompasses a wide range of backgrounds, serving affluent areas like Johnson County with a median Area Deprivation Index (ADI) of less than 30, as well as areas like Wyandotte and Jackson Counties, where many poorly resourced neighborhoods have ADI scores of 90+. Additionally, 35% of the Kansas population resides in rural or frontier counties.

To ensure that our community feels respected, valued, and empowered to participate in research, the ORE oversees an extensive program of community partnerships. The network includes religious centers, senior centers, community clinics, English and Spanish-language local media, and more, for bi-directional communication. We have had relationships with many of these partners for over 5 years, and have evolved to include shared decision-making, formal contracts, and pooled resources.

►
Research Education Component

Educational and Training Growth in ADRD: The University of Kansas Brain Health Training Program (BHTP) is a cohesive and comprehensive research training pipeline that spans undergraduate education through junior faculty development in aging and dementia research. The BHTP provides advanced research didactics, experiential learning opportunities, and professional development support for our workforce. The BHTP is a natural outgrowth of the KU ADRC’s solid base of educational programming, created in recent years, and further expands upon it with new initiatives and stronger ties with other organizational training activities. ADRC leaders are committed to a sustained effort to grow the ADRD-focused education and training programs. For instance, in the last 5 years, we have dramatically increased the number of NIH career development awardees within the ADRC from 1 in 2011 to 7 current trainees holding K-awards.

The organization of the BHTP across training levels and funding sources allows us to grow more strategically and sustainably in a comprehensive and unified manner. Our growth to date has been “opportunistic” as we have leveraged a variety of funding streams and worked to weave together various educational programs. We have achieved much success by aligning research, financial, and training resources of the KU ADRC and other organiziational resources to pursue trainees.

►
Neuroimaging Core

The KU ADRC Neuroimaging Core (NI) is under the direction of Robyn Honea, PhD and is housed on the KU SOM campus across various offices. The Neuroimaging Core supports investigation of aging and dementia through several imaging methodologies. KU ADRC research-dedicated scanning occurs at the Hoglund Brain Imaging Center (HBIC). A major goal of the HBIC is to integrate structural and functional approaches for the assessment of the brain in both health and disease. It houses a 3T Siemens Skyra whole body MRI system capable of high resolution structural and functional MRI, MR spectroscopy, and diffusion and perfusion imaging. Imaging data are stored and archived using the XNAT system. The XNAT system is supervised by the HBIC and the KU ADRC Neuroimaging Core. The ADRC NI Core hosts an imaging storage and analysis server, including Matlab, SPM, AFNI, Freesurfer, etc., as well as customized pipelines for neuroimaging quality control and analysis.

►
Biomarker Core

This core performs fluid biomarker testing with an emphasis on AD and metabolism-relevant biomarkers. It also provides molecular-biochemistry support to investigators with an emphasis on mitochondrial biology. Mitochondrial assessments include mitochondrial genetic sequencing, mitochondrial respiratory chain function determinations, the application of mitochondrial biomarkers, and the development of novel mitochondrial biomarkers. The Core is directed by Dr. Swerdlow. The Biomarker Core labs have the following major equipment:

  1. KUMC: six tissue culture incubators, hypoxia chamber, three biosafety cabinets, phase contrast microscope with fluorescence laser, clinical centrifuge, Beckman Allegra centrifuges, two Eppendorf microcentrifuges, liquid N2 storage systems, multiple refrigerators/-20 freezers/five -80 freezers, water baths, PCR and Real Time PCR thermocyclers, microwave, three spectrophotometers, electrophoresis power supplies, Chemidoc Imager, Isotemp Incubators, two Oroboros oxygraph, Seahorse XFe96, Seahorse XF96 Pro, Seahorse mini, cytation one imaging platform, BioRad ddPCR equipment, nanopore sequencer, fluorescence plate reader, fume hood, sonicator, homogenizers, nitrogen cavitation chamber, wet/semidry/dry gel electrophoresis transfer equipment, Shimadzu HPLC equipment. For fluid biomarker assessments the Core also owns and maintains Lumipulse and Quanterix SIMOA instruments.
  2. KULC: major equipment includes an Affymetrix GeneChip System including a hybridization oven 640, fluidics station 450, and genechip scanner 3000 7G, which is operated with the latest version of Affymetrix GeneChip Command Console (AGCC); an Applied Biosystems 7500 fast real-time PCR system; a Beckman Biomek NX laboratory automation workstation; an Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer; a Nanodrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer; and an Arcturus PixCell IIe laser capture microdissection (LCM) system.

Center for African American Health | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Nicole Garner

Launched in July 2023, the Center for African American Health is a community-led, community – based, academic center dedicated to improving health and well-being among Black and African American individuals. Aligned with the mission of the University of Kansas Medical Center and The University of Kansas Health System, the Center partners with local communities to identify challenges, close gaps, and support practical solutions that lead to better health. The Center’s work is grounded in four key pillars: Service, Education, Research, and Outreach & Advocacy.

  • Service includes community engagement, navigation, referrals, and coordination of care.
  • Education focuses on mentorship, training, and preparing a future healthcare workforce.
  • Research is centered on community-informed studies that reflect real-life needs and promote better outcomes.
  • Outreach & Advocacy amplifies local voices and ensures information, access, and resources are brought directly to the communities we serve.

Though rooted in improving health outcomes for African American communities, the Center works in collaboration with all groups striving to overcome obstacles to care. Developed through deep engagement with residents in Wyandotte and Sedgwick counties, the Center serves individuals of all ages and backgrounds with a shared commitment to healthier, stronger communities.

►
Center for Children’s Healthy Lifestyles & Nutrition (CHLN) | v2024.05 | Point(s) of Contact: Ann Davis

The Center for Children’s Healthy Lifestyles & Nutrition (CHLN) is a leader in the local, regional, and national movement to prevent and treat childhood obesity. Research currently conducted in the center includes numerous NIH funded studies of the assessment of genetic, physiologic, behavioral, and policy related influences on children’s healthy lifestyles. The Center serves as an academic hub for research through funding of pilot grants, research staff, student and postdoctoral training programs, academic seminars, and infrastructure support for researchers. The Center is jointly supported by Children’s Mercy Kansas City (CMKC) and the University of Kansas Medical Center and is located on the first floor of CMKC’s Don Chisholm Building. The Center is a 14,000 ft² facility designed to support clinical and bench research, individual clinical and group educational interventions, as well as offices for faculty and research staff. The Center’s 800 ft² demonstration kitchen features four prep stations, each with a GE Profile refrigerator and microwave. The kitchen contains four oven/stove/exhaust hood combinations and two dishwashers. The 500 ft2 wet lab features extensive countertop space, an exhaust hood and a -80-degree freezer. Testing rooms contain an indirect calorimeter, treadmill, and DEXA. Clinical exam rooms and a waiting room are also available. The Center’s 2,400 ft² exercise facility features treadmills, stationary bicycles, elliptical trainers, and weight machines, and has a large area for group physical activity. Locker rooms, showers, and laundry facilities are also available. The Center provides conference room facilities for 10-50 attendees.

►
Center for Interprofessional Practice, Education & Research (CIPER) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Serra Goodman

The Center for Interprofessional Practice, Education and Research at the University of Kansas Medical Center promotes collaboration among students from varied health care professions to prepare them for careers in health care. Our training capitalizes on the unique roles and responsibilities of professions by highlighting the values and ethics necessary to provide and support patient or client-centered care in the current healthcare environment. KUMC’s Center for Interprofessional Practice, Education and Research program has been in existence for over 10 years. CIPER’s scope includes Salina, Wichita, Lawrence, and Kansas City, Kansas campuses.

KUMC’s involvement with the National Center for Interprofessional Practice and Education in Minnesota (NEXUS.org) has further expanded our national recognition as a leader in Interprofessional Education. The work KUMC’s center is doing to develop a national IPE Organizational Structures Survey will inform standards for designing and maintaining IPE programs nationally. In addition, we continue to spread interprofessional education practice sites to our rural and community sites.

CIPER works with groups of interprofessional faculty from each campus to plan and carry out our large Foundations of Interprofessional Collaboration over 3 years and 3 campuses. These programs are the foundational platform designed to help students and faculty learn Interprofessional competencies backed by the Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) as well as our professional accrediting bodies. In addition, we base our program on the evidence based TeamSTEPPS teaming skills. These programs impact over 1,000 students on all campuses yearly.

CIPER reports to the Vice Chancellor for Academic and Student Affairs and to a Dean’s Council to each campus. The programing components of CIPER include a Curricular, Learning in Practice, Faculty Development and Assessment, and Scholarship planning teams.

►
Center for Multiple Sclerosis Care | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Sharon Lynch, Sara Baker

The KU Center for Multiple Sclerosis Care incorporates a three-pronged approach to address the needs of those with multiple sclerosis. In 1991, Dr Sharon G. Lynch created the MS Clinic to provide comprehensive medical care for those with multiple sclerosis. Based in the Landon Center on Aging, the MS Clinic currently follows 3,000 individuals with MS from across Kansas, western Missouri, and surrounding states. The clinic neurologists are supported by 3 clinical nurses, 2 pharmacists, a clinical social worker and 2 nursing assistants. The clinic space includes 5 dedicated exam rooms. Because of its location within the Landon Center, the MS Clinic can utilize an IV infusion area, a laboratory, a procedure room for minor procedures, and additional examination rooms when needed. Medical specialty services of Neuro Ophthalmology, Neurourology, and Neuroradiology are available for patients as needed. Facilities on the campus also provide ECG, EEG, EMG, Evoked Potentials, MRI, and sleep studies. The center also serves as a training site for medical students, neurology residents, and post-doctoral fellows in MS and Neuroimmunology.

The MS Clinic shares 5,000 ft² of space with the KU MS Achievement Center, a program that provides wellness services for those with progressive forms of MS. Dr Lynch led the development of this program in 1998 and is the Medical Director. Currently 80 individuals attend weekly, receiving education, psychological and social support, and physical and occupational therapy. Education and support services are also provided to caregivers. Led by a dedicated executive director, services are provided by a social worker, and physical and occupational therapists. The MS Achievement Center also serves as a training site for occupational and physical therapy, therapy assistant, and social work students.

The KU Center for MS Care participates in numerous multi-center clinical trials evaluating the use of medications for the treatment of MS, Neuromyelitis Optica, and other autoimmune diseases. These medications address disease modification or symptom management. In addition, many investigator-initiated trials are conducted, with a particular emphasis in the pathology of MS, psychological, cognitive, and emotional aspects of MS, and improvement in physical function. Dedicated space at the Landon Center and staff, including 3 study coordinators and 2 research assistants are available for conducting research. The research space includes storage of drug supplies, including refrigerators and a -70 C freezer. Center staff participate in quarterly meetings with a regional group of MS researchers to discuss and collaborate in numerous research activities. These researchers have a range of areas of expertise including neurology, urology, psychology, neuropsychology, pathology, medical physics, MRI, and occupational, physical and speech therapy. The research team partners with the Hoglund Brain Imaging Center and the KU Eye Clinic to provide MRI’s, other imaging processes, and visual assessments. Many MS Clinic patients and MS Achievement Center participants take part in research activities.

►
Center for Physical Activity & Weight Management | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: John Jakicic

This Center conducts research to promote physical activity and nutrition for the prevention and treatment of overweight, obesity and related comorbidities in children, adults, and special populations. Additionally, the Center supports the University of Kansas Weight Management Programs, a medically supervised weight management clinic and clinical research site that has been serving the community for over 30 years. Three laboratories and an administrative site are located at both the University of Kansas Lawerence Campus and the University of Kansas Medical Center. The Center uses energy balance approaches and behavioral strategies in both in laboratory and out-patient research and clinical programs. A whole-room calorimeter provides state-of-the-art measures of energy expenditure and substrate utilization. Given the rural nature of Kansas, the Center is active in the development of techniques for remote delivery of interventions and data collection.

►
Clinical Research Center (CRC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Mary Damewood

The University of Kansas Clinical Research Center is a unique regional resource supported by the Johnson County Education and Research Triangle (JCERT) initiative, which is a 1/8th cent sales tax passed in 2008 to create economic stimulus through new facilities for clinical research, animal health, engineering, business, science, and technology. The KU Clinical Research Center has 82,000 ft² in the beautiful suburban community of Fairway, Kansas. The CRC offers easy access to an ambulatory patient setting located near major highways and interstates with convenient parking for study participants. The CRC is home to the Fairway Clinical and Translational Science Unit, The University of Kansas Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center, and Phase I trial operations of the University of Kansas Cancer Center.

►
Diabetes Institute | v2023.05 | Point(s) of Contact: John Thyfault, Lindon Giesen

Formed in 2007, the KU Diabetes Institute's mission is to advance research leading toward prevention and control of diabetes, as well as an eventual cure for the disease. Researchers and clinicians from the University of Kansas Medical Center, the University of Kansas-Lawrence, and the KU School of Medicine-Wichita form the core of the Institute and are engaged in a wide range of basic science, translational and clinical research projects centering around diabetes and its complications. The Institute is closely partnered with the Cray Diabetes Self-Management Center, which provides excellent clinical care, education to patients with diabetes and their families, and is a partner in clinical and translational research.

The KU Diabetes Institute is focused on all forms of diabetes research, including prediabetes, type 1, metabolic disorders closely related to diabetes and type 2 diabetes; and is active in outreach and education of diabetes and its complications. The Institute maintains excellence in basic and clinical studies of autoimmunity, diabetes complications, metabolism, obesity, exercise, nutrition, epidemiology, psychosocial costs of diabetes, and parental care of children and families with diabetes. KU scientists and clinicians work to discover the intricacies of islet biology, provide new interventions to halt the progression of the disease and its complications, and inspire healthy behaviors.

The Institute assists faculty in obtaining outside funding for diabetes research in both administrative guidance and peer-review. The Institute periodically provides pilot research grants to KU scientists to initiate novel studies that have promise to attract funding from private and governmental sources. We provide in-house and external review of research proposals in addition to providing intellectual support for designing research projects, obtaining regulatory approval, and effectively using the cores and infrastructure provided on campus for research linked to diabetes. Annually, we provide travel grants to assist staff and trainees with travel to scientific meetings.

The Institute has organized and funded scientific meetings focusing on basic science and evolving clinical research. In-house scientists and trainees attend a monthly informal chalk-talk to present research ideas and preliminary data. The Director of the Institute works with KU Endowment to bring in new sources of revenue and to expand the available gifted funds.

►
Evidence-Based Practice, Outcomes & Impact Center (EPIC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Reem Mustafa

The Evidence-Based Practice, Outcomes and Impact Center is one of approximately 10 centers nationwide to receive designation by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality as an Evidence-Based Practice Center. Researchers in EPIC use comprehensive and advanced health research qualitative and quantitative methods to conduct systematic reviews, meta-analysis, meta-regression and meta-narrative synthesis in order to inform policy makers and guideline panels. EPIC collaborates with federal and state agencies, professional associations and societies, and foundations. Our reviews synthesize the evidence from research studies and assess the quality of that evidence for clinicians, patients, guideline developers, policymakers, purchasers, payors, researchers, and other health care decision-makers and stakeholders.

Areas of Expertise and Service

  • Evidence syntheses that provide the least biased and most precise results for specific questions and lead to evidence-based practice, public health and policy decisions. Evidence syntheses also ensure that resources are not wasted pursuing questions that have already been answered and will create future research agendas by identifying knowledge gaps.
  • Natural experiment design and complex data analyses that allow the unbiased estimation of the effect of a program or policy using administrative claims or survey data. This is achieved by the application of a wide variety of statistical methods (instrumental variables, difference-in-differences, panel data analysis, regression discontinuity, synthetic controls) to approximate natural experiments.
  • Decision analyses that allow for a systematic, quantitative and visual approach to addressing and evaluating the important choices that different groups in health care systems face.
  • Advise on study methods, including randomized controlled trials, observational studies, surveys and qualitative research.
  • Support for the educational goals of different graduate medical education and graduate education programs by offering research electives and practicum experience.
►
ECHO Data Coordinating & Operations Center (DCOC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Jo Wick, Megan Tremblay

The Environmental influences on Child Health Outcomes (ECHO) Data Coordinating and Operations Center (DCOC) for the NIH IDeA States Pediatric Clinical Trials Network (ISPCTN) actively supports clinical trial activity by facilitating development, conduct, and results dissemination of multicenter trials focused on rural and medically disadvantaged children. Additionally, the ECHO DCOC empowers researchers, clinicians, and community stakeholders in IDeA states by providing them with the necessary training and support to build their pediatric clinical research capacity. Finally, the center emphasizes the importance of community engagement. The ECHO DCOC will foster collaboration with communities, along with nonprofit and professional societies, to ensure that clinical trials are culturally relevant, rigorously designed, and have a significant impact on child health outcomes. The Center builds upon the outstanding foundation of policy and procedures developed in the first two cycles of the network to further increase academic productivity and enhance the identification, development, execution, and results dissemination of high quality pediatric clinical trials in these areas. ECHO DCOC integrates Quality by Design; continuous quality improvement; real-time goals, objectives, indicators, and targets monitoring; multi-faceted professional development; community research engagement and literacy; and learning collaborative approaches to ISPCTN clinical trial operations and capacity-building. This initiative promises to increase access to clinical trials for a wider range of children, while strengthening pediatric research capabilities in rural areas. Ultimately, the goal is to deliver high-quality clinical trials that generate valuable knowledge and lead to improved health outcomes for children across the United States and beyond.

►
Frontiers Clinical & Translational Science Institute | v2023.06 | Point(s) of Contact: Julius Leary, Jennifer Whitaker

Frontiers Clinical and Translational Science Institute at the University of Kansas is the home for Clinical and Translational Research for the state of Kansas and western Missouri. Since 2011, Frontiers has been funded by a $27 million grant from the NIH’s National Center for Advancing Translational Science (NCATS) Clinical and Translational Science Award (CTSA) program. Administratively centralized at the University of Kansas Medical Center, Frontiers’ partners include academic institutions (the University of Kansas (Lawrence, Wichita and Salina campuses), Kansas City University (Kansas City and Joplin, Mo. campuses), Kansas State University, and the University of Missouri-Kansas City), healthcare systems (Children’s Mercy Kansas City, St. Luke’s Health System and The University of Kansas Health System), and numerous community organizations throughout the region.

Frontiers employs a membership model that is open and free to all investigators working in clinical and translational sciences at the listed partner institutions. Frontiers has eight service cores that provide consultation and support in the following areas: Community and Collaboration, Team Science, Biostatistics and Research Methods, Regulatory Support, Genomics, Informatics, Implementation Science, Recruitment, Pre & Post-doctoral training, Early Career development, and Science Communication services. There are five Clinical Trial Service Units (CTSUs) in the Frontiers system that provides space and clinical services related to clinical trials in the region.

Frontiers hosts and co-sponsors hundreds of events throughout their catchment area, including: an annual Research Symposium, biannual Mock Study sections, monthly Research and Discovery Grand Rounds, and annual community vaccine events with 3,000+ attendees. Frontiers supports pilot funding across multiple focus areas and to date have awarded over $3 million dollars to 200+ pilot projects.

►
Hoglund Biomedical Imaging Center | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Laura Martin, Swati Levendovszky

The HBIC occupies a free-standing research-based imaging facility on the KUMC campus and provides outstanding imaging capabilities to complement the existing biomedical research community at the University of Kansas. Clinical space is also available in the HBIC. This includes a patient waiting area, consultation room, changing suite, patient preparation room, and neuropsychology testing room. An examination room for clinical procedures adjacent to the MRI is available for physical examinations, neurological examinations, blood draws and processing, urine sampling, height and weight measurements, balance testing, infusions, and providing special diets. The examination room is equipped with general nursing supplies and phlebotomy chair. Finally, a cognitive testing room is located adjacent to the examination room and scanning facilities, equipped with paper and computer-based testing capabilities.

MRI data are transferred to and stored on a network server running XNAT (Extensible Neuroimaging Archive Toolkit), an open-source imaging informatics platform managed by KUMC Information Resources. Our network-based analysis server (HBIC-SYNAPSE) has many neuroimaging software packages installed. In addition, Siemens Syngo.via server and MMWP workstation are available for offline analysis and exploration of MR imaging data. Networked file servers provide constant hardware backups of stored data through mirrored storage systems and daily tape backups are also performed. Weekly tape backups are stored off site for additional protection of research data. The network is managed by KUMC's Information Resources who provides installation, training, and maintenance on all information systems. The local area network is connected to a switched, 1 Gigabit Ethernet backbone that provides high speed Internet access through the KUMC Internet-2 communication network. KUMC is a member of the Kansas Research and Education Network (KanREN, Inc.) which provides access to the commodity Internet (Internet 1), Internet 2 via the Great Plains Network (GPN), and connectivity to other Kansas educational/research institutions and hospitals. Most recently, the KanREN network was used to create a peering network between the University of Kansas-Lawrence, the University of Kansas Medical Center, and the KU School of Medicine-Wichita. Setting up the peering network is the first step to provide seamless access to systems used by faculty, staff, students, and researchers spanning the campuses including the Advanced Computing Facility (ACF) located at the KU Lawrence campus. KUMC has had a solid track record of publications and NIH studies investigating brain imaging and connectivity in relation to metabolic dysfunction in human participants. Additional HBIC details are provided in the Shared Research Resources section.

Institute for Advancing Medical Innovation (IAMI) | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Scott Weir

The Institute for Advancing Medical Innovation (IAMI) serves as a national model for philanthropy, industry, and universities to collaborate in advancing university innovations in life sciences. The IAMI vision is to address the unmet medical needs of pediatric, adolescent, adult, and elderly patients living with diseases including cancer and rare diseases through the development of paradigm-changing medical innovations. IAMI’s mission is to discover and develop pharmaceuticals and diagnostics with a clear path to market and to improve human health by accelerating new drug therapies and medical devices to patients. The core hypothesis is that the investment in high potential academic projects with industry-experienced leadership will enhance the yield of commercial products that benefit patients. IAMI engages investigators and stakeholders, educates the translational science workforce, and uses translational science tools to conduct cutting edge product development-focused translational research.

Institute for Community Engagement | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Ryan Spaulding

The University of Kansas Medical Center created and funded a centralized outreach support structure in 2003 called Health and Technology Outreach, which became the Institute for Community Engagement in 2010, to promote the community engagement and service missions of KUMC. The Institute articulates a systems approach to engagement by ensuring integration and resources needed to be responsive to the community. The various activities of the Institute contribute to strengthening community assets that contribute to achieving the mission of the medical center. The Institute administers multiple departments and major programs that contribute to the community outreach mission of KUMC, including Area Health Education Centers (AHEC), Center for Telemedicine and Telehealth, Community Relations, Continuing Education and Professional Development (CEPD), EVC Event Planning, KUMC Educational Experiences (KEE), Project Eagle (early childhood development and Head Start), Outreach Aircraft and Rural Health Education and Services (RHES). The Institute serves KU Medical Center and Kansans by acting as a resource for engagement activities conducted by all KUMC Centers, departments, faculty, staff, or students. These activities include community-based research, workforce development, public-private partnerships, community health and education, patient care, and many other domains. The Institute reports directly to the Executive Vice Chancellor of the institution and helps implement the institutional strategy for clinical, research and educational outreach across the state of Kansas. In addition to strategy, the departments listed above provide numerous outreach services throughout the state and extensively utilize distance technologies, communications, and relationships with other institutions to enhance outreach in Kansas. Faculty and staff in the Institute are very active in both rural communities of Kansas as well as Kansas City, Kansas and are available to collaborate with or advise KUMC faculty and departments on grant, research, or service projects throughout the state of Kansas.

Area Health Education Center (AHEC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Kelly Sabol

The KU Medical Center Area Health Education Center (AHEC) established in 1978 strives to improve healthcare quality in Kansas—particularly rural parts of the state—through interprofessional education, career promotion, and research support. AHEC offices in both Pittsburg and Hays provide KUMC two of only a few physical footprints in rural Kansas. The AHEC partners with communities for two primary purposes 1) to provide continuing education for physicians, nurses, and allied health professionals throughout the state, and 2) promote health careers and workforce development through several longstanding K-12 programs. In FY24, the AHEC delivered over 800 continuing education programs and events for health professions, with more than 13,000 attendees claiming continuing education credit from cities such as Chanute, Coffeyville, Girard, Hays Hutchinson, Parsons, Phillipsburg, Salina, and Smith Center, and counties as far northwest as Cheyenne County and as far southwest as Stevens County. Some of AHEC’s primary partners include the Kansas Department of Health and Environment, Midwest Transplant Network, Brain Injury Association of Kansas, Kansas Association of Sleep Professionals and The University of Kansas Health System. Rural Kansas has high poverty in southeast rural areas, a population faced with economic challenges related to downturns in farming and oil in central and northwest Kansas, and a new immigrant population associated with meat packing and other industries in southwest Kansas. The AHECs have a strong local presence in each of these regions to meet needs unique to the area. AHECs link the resources of university health science centers with local planning, educational, research, and clinical resources. The AHECs have leveraged their strong rural relationships to support recruitment and retention of rural practices in KUMC rural primary care research grants related to epilepsy, pediatric cancer, HPV immunization, smoking cessation, and other topics.

In addition to continuing education, the AHEC has been a KUMC leader in developing and growing K-12 workforce development programs for over 3,000 high school kids annually. In the 2023-2024 academic year, 1,862 Kansas K-12 students participated in 24 Health Career Promotion events. Moreover 1,302 Kansas high school students across 59 chapters are members of Kansas HOSA, which is an international program for high schoolers interested in health care careers. AHEC became the Kansas administrator of the HOSA program in 2016. A few other programs include:

In addition to continuing education, the AHEC has been a KUMC leader in developing and growing K-12 workforce development programs for over 3,000 high school kids annually. In the 2023-2024 academic year, 1,862 Kansas K-12 students participated in 24 Health Career Promotion events. Moreover 1,302 Kansas high school students across 59 chapters are members of Kansas HOSA, which is an international program for high schoolers interested in health care careers. AHEC became the Kansas administrator of the HOSA program in 2016. A few other programs include:

  • Destination: Healthcare, formally known as Journeys and Destinations- In this day-long event, high school students spend time with health care professionals from a wide range of disciplines in a small group setting to learn about their career paths and daily activities. In the past, presenters who are family physicians, athletic trainers, medical technologists, medical forensic scientists, veterinarians, pharmacists, and occupational therapists have participated.
  • Night at the Lab- This program gives students the opportunity to research medical topics and create a visual display as well as an oral presentation. Together, the students will gain valuable experience in both research skills and professional presentation skills. A statewide competition ensues culminating in a 1-day championship at KU Medical Center where medical center staff and faculty judge the presentations.

Center for Telemedicine & Telehealth (KUCTT) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Shawna Wright

The KU Center for Telemedicine & Telehealth has been developing, implementing and researching telehealth solutions for 33 years at KUMC and all across Kansas. KUCTT currently provides telemedicine consultations in a variety of specialties including primary care, specialty care, and behavioral health. The Center in 2024 received a new $1.7 million federal HRSA grant for the THINK project (TeleHealth Integration Network of Kansas). KUCTT also is the KUMC and Kansas home of the international ECHO (Extension for Community Healthcare Outcomes) initiative and reached 3,722 unique Kansas health care providers in 104 of 105 Kansas counties over the past 5 years. This has resulted in 9,601 CME/CNE/CE hours being awarded across professions in Kansas including medicine, nursing, social work/behavioral health, physical therapy, respiratory therapy, occupational therapy, and pharmacy. Internal KUMC partners include the School of Nursing, and Department of Psychiatry on HRSA-awarded grants such as ANE-NPRF, ANEW, GWEP, and BHW programs. Additionally, the Center collaborates with the KU School of Social Welfare on HRSA-funded behavioral health workforce development projects. KUCTT also provides telehealth support to NIH and Endowment grants awarded to the Pediatrics and Oncology Departments. External KUCTT partners include the Kansas Department of Commerce on their RETAINWORKS project, exploring employment as a health outcome and United Health with a $300,000, 18-month ECHO project to address UHC health priorities. Other important partners include KDHE, KDADS, Pittsburg State University, Ft. Hays State University, and many others.

She supports KUMC’s efforts to partner with the community to improve health outcomes and programming for KCK community members by responding to health promotion, health education, workforce development and research opportunities identified in the community and collaborating with The University of Kansas Health System and the Schools of Health Professions, Medicine and Nursing to advance student learning experiences. Continuing Education & Professional Development (CEPD) | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Molly Smith

The Office of Continuing Education and Professional Development at KUMC was founded in 1909 and is dedicated to supporting the continuous growth of healthcare professionals across Kansas and beyond, with a strong emphasis on interprofessional collaboration and learning. The KUMC CEPD office is one of the only remaining academic or health system CME and CNE provider programs in Kansas. In 2023, the CEPD office received Joint Accreditation which is a combination of medicine, nursing and pharmacy accreditation and will enhance KUMC’s CE efforts while also supporting interprofessional education (IPE). The CEPD office also holds providerships in Dental, Physician Assistant, American Psychology Association, ACHA-Administrative Care, ACHA-Resident Care, Dietary, and Social Work continuing education. The office of CEPD collaborates closely with clinical departments and The University of Kansas Health System to identify educational gaps and learning needs across various healthcare fields to develop targeted educational plans such as large symposia, on-demand learning, online courses, and regularly scheduled series (RSS) such as journal clubs and grand rounds. In 2023, the Office of CE delivered over 1,000 continuing education activities for health professionals with more than 4,000 unique health care providers claiming continuing education credit from cities and counties across Kansas. These were across 66 conferences and over 50 RSS through programs like Expert Strategies in Endoscopy, Gastrointestinal and Liver Disorders; Neuromuscular Review Course; Advanced Practice Provider Symposium; Advances in the Treatment of Hematologic Malignancies and Cellular Therapeutics; KC Live Endoscopy; Cardiovascular Updates Symposium; Kidney Transplantation Update Symposium; Women’s Health Symposium; and Current Concepts in Concussion Management, to name only a few. In addition, the CEPD partners with or serves as the CME provider for several external partners including Lawrence Memorial Hospital, Johnson County Community College, KC ECHO Society, and Neurosurgical Society of America.

KUMC Educational Experience (KEE) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Tereasa Gilmore

The KEE office was developed beginning in 2016 by the Vice Chancellors for Research, Compliance, Human Resources and Community Engagement to onboard and track visiting learners on the KUMC campus. This monitoring was needed to better screen visiting learners, ensure compliance with labor laws, and enhance campus safety. Today it is the official KUMC onboarding for virtually all K-12, undergraduate and graduate visiting learners from external high schools and universities and aligns with university Visitor Policies. These include applicable campus safety, HIPAA, EHS, legal and human resources regulations. A website was developed with an application portal housed in KUMC’s REDCap system. The application and REDCap portal ensure a standardized process for interested students, while also providing embedded compliance training and other safety requirements, such as immunization attestation and background checks. Visiting learners primarily volunteer in basic science research labs and clinical research areas such as Cell Biology, Internal Medicine and Pathology for up to 12 calendar months but also may volunteer in administrative or other university learning spaces. By entering KUMC areas through the KEE system, non-KUMC visiting students are provided with the appropriate compliance training for the area in which they will volunteer, sign HIPAA and confidentiality forms, receive a temporary campus badge and receive other necessary information for being in KUMC buildings. Key internal compliance partners for the KEE system include the university badge office, General Counsel’s office, Human Resources, Environment Health and Safety office, Occupational Health and others. The majority of KEE learners are ages 16-19 and come from Johnson County, Kansas high schools, including Blue Valley, Shawnee Mission and Olathe. Many visiting learners at the undergraduate level come from KU, UMKC, KCU and Rockhurst. KEE averages roughly 300 applications annually with approximately 200 of those being completed with a student placement. In 2024 through September KEE had completed 196 student placements with an additional 88 applications in progress.

KUMC Events | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Perry Swinton-Ginsberg

The KUMC Events team primarily supports the executive vice chancellor (EVC) key university events in all aspects of event planning, coordination and management. The team also supports the broader KUMC community through event consultation, leadership, campuswide collaboration, resource-sharing and other support. By providing these services, the Events Team ensures high-quality events that reflect positively on the EVC office and KUMC. They also promote consistency in standards, communications, branding, policy compliance and budgeting. In 2023, only 37% of KUMC room reservations were for credit classes. The other 9,376 reservations were meetings, conferences, lectures, receptions and other gatherings hosted by KUMC or The University of Kansas Health System departments. A few examples of critical university events include Hooding & Recognition Ceremonies, Emeriti Lunch, Bohan Lecture, Faculty Promotion Recognition Breakfast, KBOR campus visits, and government relations visits. Other responsibilities for the events team are to ensure event quality and safety include screening events for policy compliance, parking arrangements, building access, security preparation, ADA compliance and many other activities. The Events Team partners with many internal departments to conduct these operations including Communications, Continuing Education, Emergency Management, Environmental Health & Safety, Facilities Management, Public Safety, Parking Services, KU Cancer Center, KU Endowment, Office of the Chancellor, and others.
