Project Eagle | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Lisa London

Since 1989, Project Eagle has provided early childhood development education and home visiting services to young children and pregnant women, along with their families in Kansas City, Kansas and is KUMC’s primary physical footprint in downtown KCK. In 1994, through a federal grant award, PE became one of 17 national Early Head Start (EHS) sites. In 2010, services expanded to offer Educare KC center-based early childhood education and in 2014 expanded again to provide Head Start preschool services. 100% of families served through Project Eagle reside in Wyandotte County and its care and education programs are provided at no cost to the participant children and families. Approximately 85 KUMC employees are located at Project Eagle and in the last 9 years, a total of 5,873 pregnant women, families and children have been served across four key programs including Connections, Family Resource Center, Early Head Start Home Visiting and Educare KC Head Start. A wide variety of services from these programs are provided to children and families, including 14 full day/full year classrooms for toddlers and infants, early childhood screening and referrals, parenting education, 90-minute home visits for parent skills training, dry good pantry and many other services. Project Eagle is also home to a Vibrant Health location that provides services to Project Eagle and other families in the community. In addition to Project Eagle’s federal funding, it has many, many other sponsors and partners in the community such as Children’s Mercy Hospital and Clinics, Church of the Resurrection, Community Health Council of Wyandotte County, Cornerstones of Care, Crosslines Delta Dental of Kansas, Hall Family Foundation, Healthy Blue KC, Kansas City, KS Community College, KC Healthy Kids, Kansas Department of Children and Families, Ronald D. Deffenbaugh, Sr. Foundation, Security Bank, Stanley H. Durwood Foundation, United Healthcare, and many others. Project Eagle is 100% supported by extramural funding, mostly federal grants.

►
Rural Health Education & Services (RHES) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Joyce Grayson

Located at SOM-Wichita, RHES administers a variety of programs, services, and initiatives and has served 92% of Kansas’ counties. These programs include: 1) Kansas Bridging Plan (KBP), a loan forgiveness program designed to encourage primary care, psychiatry, and OB/GYN resident physicians to practice in rural Kansas. There are currently loan forgiveness slots for primary care (14), psychiatry (3), and OB/GYN (3) residents. Each slot is for up to $10,000 and requires a 3-year practice obligation in a rural Kansas county. KBP has enrolled 420 resident physicians into the program and 83% of KBP physicians continued to practice in Kansas after their service obligation was completed, making it one of KUMC’s most successful rural placement programs; 2) Kansas Recruitment and Retention Center (KRRC) provides front-line recruitment services using best practices to Kansas healthcare organizations while also fostering a workforce pipeline of healthcare professionals including physicians, oral health providers, advanced practice providers, nurses, allied health and behavioral health professionals. Since 2004, KRRC has placed 378 providers in 72 Kansas counties and is currently working with 60 Kansas healthcare organizations to recruit for 330 positions; 3) Kansas Career Opportunities (KCO), the largest rural healthcare career fair in Kansas. In 2024, KCO events occurred in Kansas City, Wichita, and Salina. Over 300 resident physicians and students (medical, nursing, allied health, behavioral health) attended a KCO event and spoke with 45 healthcare organizations; and 4) Kansas Locum Tenens (KLT) is a temporary coverage service that engages resident physicians, faculty, and practicing physicians for short and long-term coverage in rural Kansas hospitals and clinics. KLT providers cover for physicians needing time off, short-staffing, and enhanced work-life balance by lessening call time. In FY24, KLT filled 68 temporary coverage requests and provided 170 days of coverage. RHES partners with KDHE’s State Office of Primary Care and Rural Health, Kansas Academy of Family Physicians, Kansas Hospital Association, and Community Care network of Kansas, and is a member of the national 3RNET organization. Internally at KUMC, the office works very closely with the Schools of Nursing and Medicine and multiple individual departments.

►
Institute for Reproductive & Developmental Sciences (IRDS) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Brandi Miller, Stacy Oxley, Michael Soares

The Institute for Reproductive and Developmental Sciences (IRDS) seeks to prevent disease and promote health in children and adults by focusing on the earliest stages of life. A unique blend of clinical, translational, and basic science research leaders with wide-ranging expertise, the IRDS brings together research laboratories dedicated to improving health and quality of life through scientific investigation. Our research focuses on fertility and infertility, developmental origins of health and disease, and epigenetics and stem cell biology. Our scientists are outstanding and internationally renowned with expertise ranging from epidemiology to genetics and molecular biology.

The IRDS is organized into two centers with overlapping research interests:

  • Center for Reproductive Sciences
  • Center for Organogenesis, Vascular and Perinatal Research

Research efforts of the centers include basic, translational, and clinical research. Furthermore, the centers are highly interactive. Programs in faculty development, postdoctoral training, and graduate education are key activities of the Institute and its membership.

►
Center for Reproductive Sciences

The Center for Reproductive Sciences (CRS) at the University of Kansas Medical Center focuses on fertility regulation, infertility treatment and diseases of the reproductive tracts associated with infertility. Research and clinical expertise in reproductive endocrinology provide a rich and diverse foundation for investigations in gonadal biology, contraception, embryo development and implantation, as well as diseases of the reproductive tract including endometriosis, adenomyosis, polycystic ovarian syndrome, and uterine fibroids. The overall objective of the CRS is to advance research in these areas, better educate the lay public on these topics and provide outcomes that will guide patient care.

►
Center for Organogenesis, Vascular & Perinatal Research

The quality of postnatal life has its origins in the womb. Scientists in the Center for Organogenesis, Vascular and Perinatal Research seek to understand how maternal physiology and pathology impact fetal development and program postnatal health and disease. We foster multi-investigator research efforts through collaborative research, coordinating meetings, and disseminating information. A major focus of the center is bridging basic science with clinical and translational research in the context of developmental, perinatal and vascular disorders and maternal health.

►
Jared Grantham Kidney Institute (JGKI) | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Lyn Harris

The KUMC Jared Grantham Kidney Institute is an internationally recognized world-class, research center comprised of 42 faculty investigators representing eight School of Medicine departments, including Internal Medicine, Molecular and Integrative Physiology, Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Anatomy and Cell Biology, Pathology and Laboratory Medicine, and Pharmacology, Toxicology and Therapeutics, and two from the School of Health Professions (Clinical Laboratory Sciences and Dietetics and Nutrition). A major emphasis of the Institute is polycystic kidney disease (PKD) research. The JGKI is home to the Kansas PKD Research and Translation Core Center, which is funded by a U54 grant from the NIDDK. The Kidney Institute also has interactions with the NCI-Designated KU Cancer Center and Liver Center and collaborates with other nearby entities including the Department of Molecular Biosciences at KU-Lawrence, the KC Veterans Administration Hospital, Children’s Mercy Hospital, UMKC and the Stowers Institute for Medical Research, all in Kansas City or nearby. Kidney Institute investigators occupy open-access laboratory space on two floors of Wahl Hall East and West, providing clinician-scientists and basic-scientists opportunities to closely interact on joint research projects and clinical trials. Research strengths in the Kidney Institute include polycystic kidney disease, glomerular development and disease, bone-kidney interactions, renal transport physiology, and health outcomes research.

►
Juntos: Center for Advancing Latino Health | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Mariana Ramirez

Juntos! (Spanish for “together”) is a center focused on building community-academic partnerships to generate, translate, and disseminate research findings toward the elimination of health gaps experienced by Latinos. Juntos! collaborates with a wide network of stakeholders serving Latinos in communities across Kansas, including safety net clinics, health coalitions, and social service and faith-based organizations. Through these collaborations on a variety of research and service projects, Juntos! has served thousands of Latino Kansans. Juntos! has six bilingual research staff who work with researchers and community members at the earliest stages of project conceptualization to enhance Latino community engagement and improve the cultural and linguistic quality of research projects. Specifically, Juntos! provides expert input to develop bilingual research and recruitment materials, qualitative methodologies, and participant engagement.

►
Kansas Center for Implementation Science COBRE | v2026.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Christie Befort

Based at KU Medical Center, the Kansas Center for Implementation Science (KCIS) is a Center of Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) supported by the National Institutes of Health through a $11.5 million grant that will continue building KU’s long history of research initiatives. Implementation science is an emerging field of research that specifically focuses on identifying the best approaches to integrating evidence-based practices into routine clinical care.

The goal of KCIS is to bridge the gap between research and practice. The new center will support investigators who are developing and testing implementation approaches designed to achieve evidence-based care for all populations.

►
Community Engagement & Outreach Core

Community Engagement and Outreach Core | Point(s) of Contact: Sarah Kessler

Strategies to engage with patients, families, caregivers, neighborhoods, and communities are essential to conduct implementation research. Many investigators lack exposure, education and training in how to conduct research with vs. on patients and communities and therefore default to ineffective engagement. To mitigate this ineffectiveness, investigators must expand their collaboration and include individuals, organizations and community-embedded facilitators who have established prerequisite trust. Investigators are often unaware of these resources. The vision for the Community Engagement and Outreach Core is to offer a comprehensive suite of services and training opportunities tailored to the specific needs of each project and community population.

►
Pragmatic Implementation Science Methods Core

Pragmatic Implementation Science Methods Core  | Point(s) of Contact: Ed Ellerbeck

Regardless of their research training or inherent talent, the learning curve for new investigators in implementation science can be steep. The Pragmatic Implementation Science Methods Core will provide COBRE and other KU Medical Center investigators the coordinated, interdisciplinary support that is critical to success in this complex field. Our core’s team science approach will increase the likelihood of successful execution of research projects and better prepare project leads for working in the collaborative research environment that is critical to implementation science.

►
Kansas Center for Metabolism & Obesity Research COBRE (KC-MORE) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: John Thyfault, Seven Weinman

The Kansas Center for Metabolism and Obesity Research (KC-MORE), based at KU Medical Center, is a Center of Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) supported by the National Institutes of Health. A five-year, $12 million grant helps the center build on KU's long history of research achievements in the areas of nutrition, obesity, metabolism, diabetes and fatty liver disease. KC-MORE brings together existing research programs, new state-of-the-art scientific core facilities, pilot funding for junior faculty and training opportunities to develop new approaches to the prevention and treatment of obesity and the reduction of obesity-related disease. The theme of our COBRE and support of our cores sets the stage for KU Medical Center to become a national leader in translational obesity, metabolism and obesity-related disease research. This center brings together existing research programs, creates critical new core facilities, trains a new generation of researchers and leverage both institutional and department resources for recruitment and research development in the areas of obesity, metabolism and obesity-related disease.

►
Cells, Tissues, Bioanalysis & Bioinformatics Core

The goal of the Cells, Tissues, Bioanalysis and Biostatistics (CTBB) core supported by the KC-MORE is to make this tedious process simple, centralized and efficient for research project leaders as well as the broader scientific community at KU Medical Center performing research on obesity, metabolism and obesity-related disease conditions.  The overall goal of the CTBB core is to support the KC-MORE by providing logistic and technical expertise in performing translational research with maximum efficiency and state-of-the-art methodology.

►
Human Energy Balance Core

The Human Energy Balance (HEB) core integrates facilities, equipment and expertise currently on the University of Kansas Medical Center campus and makes them available in a core form to support investigators who wish to perform human subject-based research and training on the prevention and treatment of overweight and obesity. This HEB core is an integral part of the KC-MORE. Available resources include senior, experienced personnel for conducting human trials of diet and exercise through a wide variety of individuals and environments (infants-older adults, non-typically developed individuals, rural populations) behavioral strategies to promote compliance and adherence, use of medications. There is an array of outcomes available such as testing body composition, fitness, strength, energy intake, microbiome, daily physical activity, resting and exercise metabolism, supervised and un-supervised exercise, and others. Similar facilities and capacities are available at both KUMC and KU-Lawrence. To facilitate participant accrual for investigations of weight management, the ongoing University of Kansas Weight Management Programs is available and provides a census of over 1,500 new patients per year with a registry of over 9,000 previous and ongoing patients.

►
Metabolism Core

Metabolism Core  | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: John Thyfault, Colin McCoin

The Metabolism (MET) core provides the KC-MORE with expertise, methodologies and equipment for the study of “metabolism” from the cell to the whole body. The MET core mission is to develop a new central MET core facility for pre-clinical models (rodents) that provides a host of key measurements, allowing for thorough metabolic phenotyping; and provide resources to investigators to quantify mitochondrial energetics and employ isotopic tracer measures of metabolism (glucose, fatty acids, etc.) in both rodent models and human participants.

►
Kansas Center for Rural Health | v2025.05 | Point(s) of Contact: Tom Mueller

The Kansas Center for Rural Health (KCRH) is a University of Kansas Medical Center entity dedicated to identifying and reducing rural health gaps and improving the rural healthcare workforce and care delivery through research, education, and service. Formally nested within the School of Medicine, but serving the entire KUMC body, the center has a physical presence on all three campuses—with faculty on the Kansas City and Wichita campuses and a dedicated office space and staff on the Salina campus. The center is comprised of a director, two associate directors, and two staff members. The center pursues its mission through two main program areas. The first is focused on education and service, where programming is focused on supporting the growth and maintenance of the broad rural healthcare workforce. The second area is research, where the center works to promote, sustain, and grow responsible rural health and healthcare research across the state. The center pursues these two primary aims via a variety of different programs and partnerships. Examples include sponsoring mission-relevant events, hosting lunch and learns, an annual speaker series, a quarterly newsletter, and a soon-to-launch series of topic and research briefs.

KCRH is complemented by the University of Kansas Rural Health Council, which serves as the KUMC faculty body supporting the center in achieving its goals. The Rural Health Council is led by a chair and structured in a series of committees focused on key topics for rural health. These include behavioral health; maternal, child, and family development; workforce/pathway; rural research; and data & informatics. Each committee has a chair and/or co-chairs and work in-concert with center leadership to pursue mission relevant goals.

►
Kansas IDeA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence (K-INBRE) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Doug Wright

The Kansas IDeA Network of Biomedical Research Excellence (K-INBRE) is a 25-year-old, NIH-funded program designed to strengthen the ability of Kansas’s investigators to compete for NIH funds by building a critical mass of junior and senior investigators, as well as undergraduate and graduate students, and post-doctoral fellows. This is accomplished by providing these individuals access to cutting edge technology within a scientific research theme. The program brings together NIH-funded mentors, trainees, and promising new investigators from ten universities across two states (University of Kansas Medical Center, University of Kansas Lawrence Campus, Emporia State University, Fort Hays University, Haskell Indian Nations University, Kansas State University, Langston University - Oklahoma, Pittsburg State University, Washburn University, and Wichita State University) to advance a major initiative to build strength in life sciences research. To date, K-INBRE has received more than $93 million in federal grants. Because of geographic considerations in our large but sparsely populated region, emerging perceptions of the power of team science, and the need for a skilled workforce, the program focuses on integration, communication, and training. For more than two decades the Kansas INBRE has provided significant benefits to the region, including training a highly skilled workforce and fostering the commercialization of scientific discoveries. K-INBRE’s support of faculty and trainees has generated an additional $260 million in research dollars awarded within our network. The K-INBRE has facilitated the dissemination of knowledge throughout Kansas and beyond via videoconferencing, symposia, and by encouraging intra- and inter-state collaborations. The K-INBRE established the first bioinformatics facility in Kansas (3 campus cores), now broadened to data science, and was instrumental to lay the groundwork for fostering translational research and the use of medical informatics. The K-INBRE has also been instrumental in facilitating industry collaborations with the academic community. It has supported research training for 1,672 undergraduates, numerous post-doctoral fellows and new faculty. The K-INBRE has also increased the participation of students from groups (rural and ethnic) lacking in scientific training and research. In 2022, 147 graduate and undergraduate students were supported by K-INBRE funds. The overall goal of this program is to strengthen research and training in NIH associated biomedical research in the State of Kansas and the region, with the aim to develop new tools, therapies, and strategies to improve human health.

►
Kansas Institute for Precision Medicine COBRE (KIPM) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Andrew Godwin

The Kansas Institute for Precision Medicine (KIPM) COBRE advances healthcare customization by promoting innovative scientific discoveries. Precision medicine is an approach that combines clinical information with unique and informative molecular information and matches this to molecularly tailored therapies. The KIPM seeks to foster precision medicine by enabling the next generation of scientists and physician/scientists in this compelling area, by shaping their research ideas into a tightly focused endeavor with a precision medicine theme and thereby making them highly competitive for national peer-reviewed funding. To achieve this, the KIPM i) provides innovative mentoring and training programs on precision medicine theme, ii) strengthens biomedical research capacity within our region by enhancing the research base and infrastructure/core capacities, and iii) supports three research cores and one community engagement resource.

►
Biomedical Engineering (BME) Core

The BME Core has two major facilities; (i) Plastics Engineering Facility (KULC) to allow for the generation of new microfluidic devices to accommodate any biomedical measurement with full process automation and support the activities of the second facility by supplying chips for the analysis of biomarkers; and (ii) liquid Biopsy Facility (KUMC), which supports the analysis of a variety of liquid biopsy markers, such as rare cells, nanoscale vesicles, and cell free molecules. Liquid biopsies provide the ability to secure disease management biomarkers in a minimally invasive manner to provide vital information to enable precision decisions on disease management. The BME Core isolates liquid biopsy biomarkers from a variety of clinical samples such as blood, saliva, urine, and others. The Liquid Biopsy Facility, which is a unique resource, uses plastic-based and specially designed microchips for the isolation of such markers as circulating tumor cells, cell free DNA, and extracellular vesicles using robotic platforms that automate the sample processing pipeline. Using the appropriate microfluidic chip, the robot can process a clinical sample for a selected liquid biopsy biomarker in a fast turnaround time with sufficient purity to submit the marker directly to several different assays such as RT-qPCR, RT-ddPCR, Western blotting, proteomic analysis (LC/MS), and Next Generation Sequencing. The Plastics Engineering Facility can generate microfluidic chips for any desired application and has in place design engineers to design chips for the intended application.

►
Biobanking & Biomarker Validation (BBV) Core

The Biobanking and Biomarker Validation (BBV) Core combines expertise and crucial resources such as the Biospecimen Repository Core Facility, the Biomarker Discovery Laboratory, and the Clinical Molecular Oncology Laboratory, to provide:

  • Centralized and uniform collection, processing and storage of tissue and body fluids and tissue-related histology services
  • Integral and comprehensive protein and nucleic acid isolation, quantitation, and molecular characterization services
  • Fully customizable molecular testing and genomic-based sequencing services.

The BBV Core centralizes essential biobanking resources and services to provide a cost-effective solution for investigators. In addition, in-kind expert technical and scientific support for molecular studies from the Core staff and directors and the use of available highly specialized research equipment and other resources help investigators conserve their research funds.

►
Quantitative 'Omics (QO) Core

The Quantitative ‘Omics Core develops and applies innovative statistical, bioinformatics, and data science methods to assist investigators. The Quantitative ‘Omics Core has experience in the analysis and interpretation of high-throughput ‘omic studies, including studies of gene expression (microarray and RNA-seq), pathway analysis, protein-DNA binding (e.g., ChIP-seq), DNA methylation, DNA variation and integrative multi-‘omic analysis. This team’s skills span the domains of biostatistics, bioinformatics and statistical ‘omics. Together with access to high-performance computing and storage for large data sets, this core helps KIPM investigators with their study design, data collection, data management, analytics, bioinformatics, and statistical needs.

The Quantitative ‘Omics Core offers help with:

  • Study design
  • Data management
  • Data visualization
  • Bioinformatics
  • Access to high-performance computing
  • State-of-the-art bioinformatics software
  • Statistical analyses
►
Patient & Community Engagement (PACE) Resource

There is a long history of mistrust between researchers and communities of color and under-resourced groups. A potential contributing factor is mistrust from researchers traditionally seeing research participants as "subjects" rather than treating them as contributors, partners, or consumers of research. Mistrust is a major hurdle to advance precision medicine. If patients do not understand why and how data about them or their families are being used in research, they are reluctant to say "yes" when asked to participate. This dynamic is changing as patients and communities are becoming more empowered and engaged in health care decisions. But many researchers lack training in how to conduct research in partnership with patients and other stakeholders. Many are unaware of the opportunity they receive for being scientists, grant recipients or clinicians.

The Patient and Community Engagement Resource offers:

  • Mentoring sessions for researchers
  • Educational opportunities on successful patient/community-researcher engagement strategies
  • Patient research representatives who offer feedback to researchers on their studies and provide patient- and community-centered perspectives to further productive engagement
  • Connections with community organizations and thought leaders
  • Awareness-raising opportunities offered by the community about the community

PACE is co-led by an academic research leader and a patient research representative. Together, these colleagues bring real-world, patient- and community-informed practices to the KIPM.

►
Kansas Intellectual & Developmental Disabilities Research Center (KIDDRC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Peter Smith, Michelle Winter

The Kansas Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities (IDD) Research Center (KIDDRC) has been funded by the National Institute of Health and Human Development for over 50 years (as P30 HD002528, and now as U54 HD090216). Throughout its history, the KIDDRC has played a major role in elucidating the causes, prevention and treatment of IDD and related secondary conditions. The center brings together researchers from the KU-Lawrence and Kansas University Medical Center campuses, as well as from the Juniper Gardens Children’s Project at the Children’s Campus of Kansas City. For more than five decades, the KIDDRC has served as a model of interdisciplinary collaboration across campuses and disciplines. KIDDRC investigators collaborate on many funded projects, including projects with other IDDRCs at Vanderbilt, UNC Chapel Hill, the University of Washington, the University of Wisconsin, Washington University in St. Louis and Johns Hopkins University/Kennedy Krieger Center. Core support includes:

►
Clinical Translational Core

The Clinical Translational Core (CTC) provides KIDDRC investigators with tools for enhancing translational research. The CTC by provides access to an integrated repository and other regional databases, by maintaining and expanding registries for access to children with well-characterized IDD and typically developing children, and by facilitating contact with community organizations and facilities that serve populations of interest to projects in the KIDDRC portfolio.

►
Preclinical Models Core

The Preclinical Models Core facilitates translational applications by assisting in developing cellular and organismal models of IDD by providing infrastructure and resources needed to create and characterize laboratory models of IDD, and by extending KIDDRC’s prior capabilities for analyzing behavior, anatomy, physiology, and gene expression.

►
Clinical Outcomes/Biobehavioral Technology Core

The Clinical Outcomes/Biobehavioral Technology Core (CBC) provides a formalized infrastructure for assisting KIDDRC investigators with the initiation, implementation, and use of biobehavioral assessments of human participants in IDD research. The objective of the CBC is to provide high quality, cost-effective support to KIDDRC research programs requiring quantitative measurement of human neurobehavioral and behavioral outcomes, as well as biological correlates.

►
Research Design & Analysis Core

The Research Design and Analysis Core supports analysis of data from both preclinical and clinical research through state-of-the-art statistical and bioinformatics methods. Appropriate scientific design and analysis is critical to the validity and impact of all research conducted within the themes of the KIDDRC.

►
Kansas Nursing Workforce Center | v2026.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Barbara MacArthur, Teresa Stenner

The Kansas Nursing Workforce Center based at the University of Kansas School of Nursing, is foundationally steeped in research, education, and policy development. The Center uses evidence-based practices to examine information, provide solutions, and generate new knowledge in three specific focus areas 1) support how nurses lead in all work settings 2) health and well-being of nurses individually and as part of the care team 3) approaches used to build, sustain, and retain the nursing workforce. The Kansas Nursing Workforce Center is dedicated to strengthening the nursing workforce by addressing supply, demand, and distribution challenges. The Center collects and analyzes workforce data, publish reports to inform stakeholders, and develops evidence-based recommendations to guide workforce development and policy decisions. The Center takes a strategic approach by forecasting workforce needs, identifying gaps, and supporting sustainable strategies to ensure an adequate and well-prepared nursing workforce.

►
Kansas PKD Research & Translation Core Center | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Darren Wallace

The Kansas PKD Research and Translation Core Center (RTCC) is supported by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (U54 DK126126) and is part of the national PKD Research Resource Consortium (PKD-RRC). The mission of the Kansas PKD RTCC is to promote PKD research by providing essential reagents, PKD mouse models, and human biomaterials, and by assisting PKD clinical investigators in the development and implement of clinical trials to improve patient outcomes. The Kansas PKD RTCC provides three biomedical research cores to support the PKD-RRC and the greater PKD research community.

►
Biomarkers & Biomaterials Core

The Biomarkers and Biomaterials Core supports the discovery, validation, and development of biomarkers for early stages of PKD. The Core maintains a repository of biospecimens including blood, urine, and urinary exosomes from individuals with early-stage ADPKD, who are enrolled in the longitudinal Early PKD Observational Cohort (EPOC) study, as well as siblings and normal individuals. Subject-level data including BUN, serum creatinine, and total kidney volume from MRI are available. The Core offers a comprehensive assortment of high-quality biomaterials including frozen and fixed tissues; primary epithelial cells derived from ADPKD and normal human kidneys; serum and plasma; individual and pooled cyst fluid; paraffin sections and histology specimens; and RNA, DNA, and cellular proteins to investigators. The Core also assists investigators in the use of in vitro models of PKD to test specific hypotheses and evaluate potential therapies. This core has been critical in providing human biomaterials to the PKD research community; and serves as an important resource for the PKD-RRC.

►
Rodent Models & Drug Testing Core

The PKD Rodent Models and Drug Testing Core generates novel mouse models for PKD research and provides reagents and services to PKD investigators at KUMC and other institutions and is an essential resource for the PKD-RRC. The Core maintains and distributes several key mouse lines to accelerate our understanding of PKD and other renal cystic disorders. It also provides expertise and experimental support in handling PKD mouse models for drug testing and in processing and analyzing tissue specimens, such as embryonic organ culture.

►
Clinical Research Core

PKD is a "therapy-ripe" disease and the number of potential targets for drug therapy increases at a phenomenal rate. Academic investigators can play a major role in translational research by evaluating potential targets and drugs and bringing promising candidates to early phase clinical trials. Thus, the goal of the Clinical Research Core is to develop a formal infrastructure to support continued growth in PKD clinical trial activity, to develop innovative tools to facilitate clinical research (including trial recruitment, biomarker monitoring, and outcomes research); facilitate investigator-initiated trials; and provide a pathway for investigators to expedite translation of novel or repurposed drug candidates to clinical trials. This is achieved by providing consultative advice on drug development, a patient registry network for clinical trial recruitment, resources, and services to conduct clinical trials, and a searchable integrated clinical data repository for observational research.

►
KU Center for Community Access, Rehab Research, Education & Service Center | v2026.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Jacob Sosnoff

KU Center for Community Access, Rehab Research, Education & Service Center (KU CARES) is dedicated to improving the health and quality of life of individuals living with disabilities. KU CARES brings together experts across disciplines to develop and implement innovative rehabilitation strategies that prevent disability, enhance function, and promote well-being. Building on KU’s strong foundation in rehabilitation science, physical and occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, audiology, and nutrition, the center will foster collaboration among researchers, clinicians, and students. By expanding rehabilitation research, supporting interprofessional education, and ensuring access to state-of-the-art interventions across Kansas and beyond, KU CARES aims to lead transformative advances that empower people with disabilities to live fuller, healthier lives.

►
Landon Center on Aging (LCOA) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Bruce Troen

Established by the Kansas Legislature in 1986 to foster improved health and health care for an aging population, the Landon Center on Aging (LCOA) is an interdisciplinary hub that conducts, sponsors, and supports the development of educational, clinical, research and community programs related to aging. The Landon Center is home to geriatrician faculty in both the Departments of Internal Medicine and Family Medicine. The Landon Center is home to a geriatric medicine clinic, seeing patients from around the community for primary and consultative care, with an interdisciplinary and interprofessional approach that not only provides a comprehensive patient assessment, but also offers a training ground for medical students, residents and fellows in an array of specialties. Clinical programs of the Department of Neurology are also housed within the Landon Center. The Landon Center encourages, promotes, and conducts research relevant to older adults and serves as the focus for aging research across the campus. The center provides facilities for a robust portfolio of research on such aging-related issues as prevention and treatment of physical decline, cognitive function, and patterns of healthcare delivery. These activities are further supported by the LCOA’s Grayhawk registry, which is a database of older adults who are interested in participating in geroscience based clinical trials. In early 2025, the registry had over 1,000 people over the age of 65. Also, within the LCOA is the Human Performance Laboratory (HPL), a 2,500-square-foot interdisciplinary research and education center dedicated to the study of age-related changes in mobility in the healthy elderly and those with age-related pathologies. The HPL has the equipment for the quantitative assessment of gait, evaluation of sit-to-stand, balance/postural stability, ankle and knee isokinetic and isometric strength, and hand kinematics. Ongoing studies are directed toward examining gait and balance in patients suffering with Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and post-stroke impairments. Landon Center collaborations include scientists from various departments within the KUMC School of Medicine, especially those in the Departments of Internal Medicine, Family Medicine, Cell Biology & Physiology, as well as with faculty and students in the bioengineering program at the University of Kansas-Lawrence and in the rehabilitation science and occupational therapy programs at the KU School of Health Professions. The Landon Center also serves a hub for community outreach programs, helping seniors stay active and engaged with fitness programs, educational workshops, and regular Brown Bag lunch talks on such topics as sleep health, navigating over-the-counter treatments for older adults, and tips and tricks on what to do when downsizing a home.

►
Human Performance Laboratory

The Human Performance Laboratory (HPL) occupies over 2,500 ft² on the first floor of the Landon Center on Aging building on the University of Kansas Medical Center campus in Kansas City, KS. The HPL is dedicated to the study of age-related changes in mobility in the healthy elderly and those with age-related pathologies. The HPL has the latest equipment for the quantitative assessment of gait, evaluation of sit-to-stand, balance/postural stability, ankle and knee isokinetic and isometric strength, and hand kinematics. Ongoing studies are directed toward examining gait and balance in people suffering with Parkinson’s disease, multiple sclerosis, and post-stroke impairments and age-related disorders. Landon Center collaborations include scientists from various departments at KUMC, especially those in the Department of Physical Therapy, Rehabilitation Science and Athletic Training, as well as with faculty and students on the University of Kansas-Lawrence campus.

Major equipment in the HPL includes an 8-camera high speed motion capture system (Motion Analysis Inc.), Delsys wireless EMG system, four AMTI 1000 force platforms, a Cybex 6000 Testing and Rehabilitation system, a Biodex Rehabilitation Treadmill, a 26-foot pressure sensitive walkway (Protokinetics, Hanover, PA), an overhead harness system, AX6 sensors, Opal wireless inertial sensors (APDM), and a servo-controlled medical treadmill (Woodway USA, Inc) for postural response testing. Data collection from the electromyography system and wireless inertial sensor system is synchronized with data collection from the motion capture system. There is an overhead harness system for participant safety and a digital video camera and memory cards to record data collections. The HPL also houses a shared neuromodulation resource center, focusing on research studies in non-invasive brain stimulation.

In addition to software licensed through the university, the HPL has licenses for Labview (National Instruments Corp. USA) for virtual instrument design, Matlab (MathWorks, Natick, MA, USA) for data acquisition and analysis, and SPSS for statistical analysis. The laboratory also has licenses on three computers (1 Dell Optiplex 745 Intel Xeon 3.3GHz 16GB RAM, 2 HP 8300 Elite Intel Core i5 3.2GHz 16GB RAM) for motion capture software processing. One computer is used for data collection and analysis, while the other two are used for analysis only. Data are initially recorded to the laboratory computer and transferred to a secured external hard drive for storage. The university maintains a secure, backed-up server for storing documents where all data will be copied after each data collection. There are also multiple printers, a projector for presentations, and video conferencing capabilities. Each graduate student has access to their own laboratory computer (HP 8300 Elite), laboratory printer, network access, video conferencing capabilities, and ample secure storage. Additional research software includes Cortex (Motion Analysis Corporation, CA, USA), Visual3D (C-Motion Inc., Germantown, MD, USA) and Microsoft Visual Studio (Microsoft, USA).

  • Motion Capture Systems- Eight, high-speed digital cameras for gait and balance assessment (Eagle System; Motion Analysis Corporation, Santa Rosa, CA) and a separate six camera upper extremity assessment system (512 cameras, Vicon Motion Systems, Denver, CO)
  • Force measurement- Embedded force platforms (AMTI, Watertown, MA) mounted into a concrete subfloor slab for isolation of kinetic signals.
  • Electromyography- Trigno Wireless EMG; (Delsys Incorporated, Boston, MA)
  • Wireless Inertial Sensor System- Mobility Lab (Opal sensors, APDM, Portland, OR)
  • Pressure sensitive walkway- 26-foot Zeno mat for determination of spatiotemporal parameters of gait and balance assessment (Protokinetics, Hanover, PA).
  • Body weight support systems- custom built
  • Isokinetic Dynamometer- Cybex (Cybex Intl, Medway, MA)
  • Medical Treadmill- Woodway (Woodway USA, Waukesha, WI)
  • Vibrating Tactors- Vibratron (Physitemp Instruments, Clifton, NJ)

Liver Center | v2026.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Steve Weinman

The primary mission of the KU Liver Center is to be a multidisciplinary intellectual focus for liver researchers by bringing the Basic Science, Translational Science, Clinical Research, Pathology, Radiology, Clinical Hepatology, and Surgery communities together. The Liver Center Director is Dr. Steve Weinman (MPI of the KC-MORE COBRE). The Center facilitates collaborations between the clinical care components of the liver community, the Liver Treatment Center, and the Center for Transplantation, in a mutually supportive relationship that will allow both clinical and research aspects of the liver enterprise to reach their full potential. The Liver Center includes both the Biospecimen Repository (The Liver Bank) and the Clinical Studies Unit. The Liver Bank is human liver tissue depository that supplies liver tissue, RNA, serum, and de-identified clinical data for biomedical research to investigators at the University of Kansas Medical Center. The Liver Center Clinical Studies Unit provides support for investigator initiated clinical research conducted by Liver Center members. The Unit has a full-time senior clinical research coordinator and provides a full array of clinical investigation services including assistance with IRB submission, GCP and HSC monitoring and support, human subject recruitment, study participant visits, human blood sample collection, and grant submission support. Current research is funded by a combination of individual NIH research grants, training grants, and a COBRE grant to the Department of Pharmacology, Toxicology and Therapeutics supporting faculty development and core facilities. Major interests of KU Liver Center investigators include Liver Toxicology, Drug-Induced Liver Injury, Alcoholic Liver Disease, Autophagy in the Liver, Viral Hepatitis, Nuclear Receptors and Drug Development. The Center also promotes research interactions though weekly Translational Research Meetings. Fatty liver is a metabolic disease associated with obesity that can lead to further liver injury (steatohepatitis and cirrhosis) and hepatocellular cancer. Fatty liver rates are on the rise in both pediatric and adult populations yet there is no known effective treatment other than diet and exercise.

►
Liver Center Biorepository

The KUMC Liver Center Biorepository provides channels to procure, store, distribute, and study human liver tissue. It currently receives support from the KUMC School of Medicine and The University of Kansas Health System. Current activities and services include collecting and banking freshly frozen tissue specimens from excess surgical material in liver transplants, resections and biopsies, processing and banking blood, serum, and urine, maintaining a sample database with extensive clinical and pathological data, and coordinating patient consent. Isolated RNA, DNA and protein may also be available upon request. We can provide a variety of tissue types including:

  • Normal
  • Liver Cancer
  • Viral Hepatitis
  • Bile Duct Diseases
  • Fatty Liver/NASH
  • Alcoholic Liver Disease
  • Autoimmune Hepatitis

Midwest Stem Cell Therapy Center (MSCTC) | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Sunil Abhyankar

The Midwest Stem Cell Therapy Center (MSCTC) was created by the Kansas Legislature in the 2013 session, with a state appropriation. The MSCTC helped establish a systematic mechanism for Kansans to receive adult stem cell therapy in the state and region and served as a coordinated center to translate basic stem cell research findings into clinical applications. The MSCTC faculty and staff include physicians, scientists, and trainees representing the fields of adult stem cell biology, neurology, oncology, hematology, cardiac and vascular, endocrine, and other sub-specialties. These individuals represent several local and regional institutions, enabling the formation of a stem cell network of knowledge and information. This synergy among various institutions also fosters productive collaborations that may result in faster translation of basic science discoveries into the clinic. The MSCTC houses an FDA- registered GMP facility with the demonstrated capability to provide clinical grade adult stem cells for use in clinical trials. Several clinical trials with adult stem cells are in the start-up phase within KUMC and external research collaborations are being discussed. In addition, cutting edge molecular stem cell research is being conducted by MSCTC scientists. These ongoing studies involve induced pluripotent stem cells, regulation of cellular differentiation, cord blood cells, as well as various transcription factors and other molecular pathways in adult stem cells. For patients interested in stem cell studies going on around the country, there is a set of "ready-made" searches that automatically search ClinicalTrials.gov for the latest studies. In addition, the MSCTC is planning to expand training postdoctoral fellows in basic research in adult stem cell biology, as well as clinicians in adult stem cell-related topics.

►
Nutrition Obesity Research Centers Research Resource Center | v2026.02 | Point(s) of Contact: John Jakicic

The University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC) Nutrition Obesity Research Centers Research Resource Center (NORC-RRC) leads, supports, and assists broad areas of the NIDDK NORC Consortium. Within these areas, the primary focus of the NORC-RRC is to support early-to-mid career investigators to lead regional, national, and international efforts related to nutrition and obesity both internally at KUMC and more broadly to implement initiates at the national level. These efforts include implementation of a Pilot and Feasibility Program to foster novel research initiatives. Moreover, this includes a NORC Scholars Program to provide intensive and focused training in nutrition and obesity research within the context of an ongoing mentoring program aimed at early-to-mid career investigators. These efforts also include additional enrichment opportunities led by the NORC-RRC and in partnership with professional organizations (e.g., The Obesity Society, etc.). The NORC-RRC also manages the NORC Consortium’s Opportunity Program that focuses on the training and mentoring of early-career investigators while also enhancing collaborative opportunities across the NORC Consortium. Through the NORC-RRC, the nutrition and obesity portfolio is being bolstered to better serve the KUMC community while also integrating KUMC within the broader and national efforts of the NORC Consortium.

►
Parkinson’s Disease & Movement Disorder Center | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Kelly Lyons

The Center offers diagnostic and treatment services for persons with Parkinson’s disease and related conditions including progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy and Lewy body dementia as well as essential tremor and other tremor disorders, hyperkinetic disorders like dystonia, chorea including Huntington's disease and tardive dyskinesia, restless legs, and others. The Center offers specialized speech, swallowing, occupational and physical therapy, pharmacy, dietetics, and social services. In addition to use of various medications, surgical interventions including deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the subthalamic nucleus, globus pallidus and thalamus for Parkinson's disease, essential tremor and dystonia, as well as MRI-guided focused ultrasound for essential tremor and Parkinson’s disease are available. We also offer botulinum toxin injections for hyperkinetic disorders and drooling. Educational information about Parkinson’s disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, multiple system atrophy, Lewy body dementia, essential tremor and other movement disorders is also provided. Various educational programs are presented each year and information about regional support groups and other programs and classes are available. The center is recognized as a Center of Excellence in clinical care, research, and outreach by the Parkinson's Foundation (Miami, FL) and works closely with the International Essential Tremor Foundation.

►
Schiefelbusch Institute for Life Span Studies (LSI) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Teresa Christenson

A freestanding institute within the University of Kansas Center for Research, the Life Span Institute commands the largest external funding support of any research center on the University of Kansas Lawrence Campus (over $46 million in income from grants, contracts and indirect costs), a rarity for behavioral sciences centers. The KU Life Span Institute brings together researchers at the intersections of education, behavioral science and neuroscience to study problems that directly affect the health and well-being of individuals and communities in Kansas, as well as across the nation and world. In addition to this internationally renowned research program, thousands of people benefit from the direct services, training and consultations provided by the KU Life Span Institute and its nine research centers and dozens of affiliated investigators. The Life Span Institute includes a central office that provides research, finance, technology, and communications support to more than 100 investigators. LSI has a successful track record of providing pre- and post-award services for many faculty on campus. The leadership team includes associate directors charged with delivering services spanning finance, pre-award, communications, information technology, and research design and analysis.

►
The University of Kansas Cancer Center | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Teresa Christenson

The University of Kansas Cancer Center is the only National Cancer Institute-designated (P30 CA168524) comprehensive cancer center in the region, and 1 of fewer than 60 in the nation, to receive this distinction. The KU Cancer Center operates as a matrix, consortium organization and includes: The University of Kansas Medical Center (KUMC), the University of Kansas Lawrence Campus (KULC), the Stowers Institute for Medical Research, and Children’s Mercy Kansas City. Currently, there are 360 members in three research programs: Cancer Biology, Cancer Prevention and Control, and Drug Discovery, Delivery, and Experimental Therapeutics. KU Cancer Center scientists use over 200,000 ft2 of laboratory space across the KUMC campus and an additional 22,000 ft2 of office space. The total KUMC research laboratory, clinical and shared resource space is more than 700,000 ft2.

KU Cancer Center provides financial and administrative support for seven shared resources: Biospecimen, Biostatistics and Informatics, Clinical Pharmacology, Flow Cytometry, Lead Development and Optimization, Nutrition, and Transgenic and Gene-Targeting. These shared resources are fully equipped to provide KU Cancer Center investigators with access to state-of-the-art research technology, equipment, and technical support that would otherwise be too difficult or expensive for individual investigators or programs to develop. KU Cancer Center shared resources occupy more than 45,000 ft2 of space located in several facilities on the KUMC campus, the KULC, The University of Kansas Hospital’s Westwood campus, the University of Kansas Clinical Research Center, and Children’s Mercy Kansas City.

►
Masonic Cancer Alliance (MCA) | Point(s) of Contact: Hope Krebill, Ashley Spaulding

The Masonic Cancer Alliance (MCA) was originally launched in 2008 as a network of hospitals, oncologists, and cancer support organizations across Kansas and western Missouri focused on fostering collaboration in cancer prevention, screening, treatment, and survivorship and to extend clinical trials, making it possible for patients to access resources and research close to home. The University of Kansas Cancer Center established the MCA as its outreach network to support research and evidence-based cancer control efforts in collaboration with health care providers and community hospitals, the majority of which serve predominately rural and medically disadvantaged populations. A membership-based alliance, the MCA is comprised of hospitals and research organizations across Kansas and western Missouri. Each year, MCA collaborates with local health providers to increase access to evidence-based programs. All MCA members have access to second opinions, consultation services, outreach programs, financial navigation, psychosocial services, and continuing education. In 2019, we were able to expand the MCA reach and type of cancer clinical trials available through the NCI’s Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP). KU Cancer Center-MCA is designated as a community site of the NCORP. In addition to our research and services for members, the MCA coordinates three regional cancer coalitions for Kansas Cancer Partnership, the Kansas comprehensive cancer control partnership funded through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The regional coalitions are made up of health care professionals and community members focused on cancer prevention efforts such as tobacco cessation, human papilloma virus (commonly referred to as HPV) vaccination, and cancer survivorship.

The MCA facilitates a comprehensive community engagement approach to reduce cancer burden by stimulating and supporting research in high priority areas, facilitating bi-directional communication between community members and cancer center leadership and researchers, and performing cancer control activities including dissemination and implementation of evidence-based interventions, public education, and influencing health policy. The MCA identifies these high priority areas by monitoring the cancer burden and needs and by engaging community stakeholders throughout the KU Cancer Center catchment area. Through this approach, MCA has a direct impact on KU Cancer Center research and cancer prevention and control strategies. The MCA also influences the institutional culture that includes a bi-directional relationship between KU Cancer Center leadership and researchers with patients and community members.

►
Masonic Cancer Alliance Mobile Medical Unit

This is a highly specialized vehicle designed to be driven throughout rural Kansas to see patients, collect specimens, conduct assessments, and complete other aspects of the clinical trial research process. The vehicle is equipped with two exam rooms, sink, wheelchair lift, lab with medical refrigerator, specimen collection area, screening room, phlebotomy equipment and chair, exam table, and Wi-Fi.

Zamierowski Institute for Experiential Learning | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Emily Diederich

The Zamierowski Institute for Experiential Learning (ZIEL) is a partnership between KU Medical Center and The University of Kansas Health System that provides advanced educational resources to create an immersive team training experience for healthcare professionals and trainees from all disciplines. ZIEL is staffed by a team dedicated to collaborating with educators to develop training programs based on proven methodologies. By creating a safe environment for practice, reflection, and innovation, the institute leverages clinicians and educators from across campus to benefit current and future patients and families. This collaborative approach ensures we are prepared to achieve world-class education, research, and care, both now and into the future.

Experiential learning at ZIEL enables individuals to apply what they have learned to concrete experiences, reflect on the encounter, and then refine future performance. By taking new knowledge and skills 'for a test drive' through experiential learning, participants can integrate complex concepts, adapt medical knowledge to nuanced cases, learn from mistakes, and generate new ideas for improving patient care. Through simulation, we recreate the key aspects of reality to provide an opportunity for experiential learning. By creating a space for repetitive practice and reflection, health care simulation ensures that students and professionals continuously hone their skills, so they are prepared to deliver the best care possible to patients.

Shared University Services
►
Research Administration & Support Infrastructure | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Paul Toler

The division of Research Administration provides oversight for research at the University of Kansas Medical Center. The units within Research Administration provide support services including grants management, clinical trials administration, contract support, training and regulatory oversight. KUMC Research Administration has dedicated resources for training and professional development to enhance research personnel skills, knowledge, and professionalism.

The office of Sponsored Programs Administration (SPA) serves as the central office for processing proposals and awards. SPA assists faculty and departmental research staff to secure external funding and ensure proper management of awarded funding. These services include but are not limited to proposal review; authorization, submission, negotiation, and acceptance of grants, subawards and funding contracts; set-up and closeout of awarded funds; and supporting investigators in their responsibility to ensure compliance with applicable federal, state, and local laws as well as sponsor regulations.

The Division of Clinical Research supports the conduct of clinical research for the University of Kansas Medical Center, including dedicated support from a Portfolio Manager, coordination of study activation processes, budget development and negotiation, regulatory guidance, quality assurance support, and training.

The Research Contracts Office reviews and negotiates industry sponsored agreements and other research-related contracts and subcontracts to ensure conformity with University policy and applicable laws and regulations.

►
Research Informatics | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Jeffrey Thompson

The Office of the Chief Research Informatics Officer is located on the 3rd floor of the Student Center on the main KUMC campus. The center has over 3,000 ft2 of office, cubicle, storage, and conference room space. Office of the Chief Research Informatics Officer provides capabilities and expertise in software engineering, data warehousing, data management, data integration, administration of clinical trial and electronic data capture systems, and cloud computing.

Research Informatics supports investigators and administrators at KUMC, affiliated organizations and external partners by providing informatics tools and expertise including: 1) high performance computing infrastructure, 2) data management and software development, 3) data integration and warehousing, 4) interventional informatics integrated with clinical workflow and patient experience and 5) business intelligence and analytical support for planning and decision making. Research Informatics spans the KUMC and the UKHS to empower researchers to use clinical systems to support research in a variety of ways. Additionally, Research Informatics provides data governance and honest broker services for distributing data sets through our Certified Honest Data Broker program, and training and consultation with investigators and their teams seeking to advance clinical research and health system improvement. This ranges from hypothesis generation to data-driven clinical trial recruitment and supporting large multi-institution observational studies.

►
Data Concierge

Research Informatics provides support through the full research lifecycle. We have a large array of services and tools, and our Data Concierge is here to connect investigators and researchers to the appropriate resources.

►
The Digital Research Platform (DRP)

The DRP at KUMC is the collective name for our HIPAA- compliant, research cloud infrastructure, which includes a centralized research data lakehouse, built on Databricks, to enable big data handling with Apache Spark and robust performance with Delta Lake. High performance computing, including GPU clusters is available from Microsoft Azure and can be scaled on demand, and machine learning lifecycle management is available from MLFlow. Dedicated research data management staff are available to help ingest new data into the environment, who use a customized version of Data Basin to facilitate and speed complex data ingestion into the lakehouse. Analytics and model building can be performed in Databricks, in Azure, or in the user’s on-prem environment.

►
HERON

The Healthcare Enterprise Repository for Ontological Narration (HERON) is an integrated clinical data repository with approximately 2 million patient electronic medical records (EMR) as well as records of patients who agree to be contacted for research, social, economic, and demographic data, death data, and clinical notes, which is a valuable resource for clinical and translational research. KUMC researchers can build a study cohort with HERON using the i2b2 (Informatics for Integrating Biology and the Bedside) software and request de-identified and identified data.

►
Green HERON

Green HERON is a highly protected health data analytic space where approved users can work with de-identified health information. Green HERON simplifies the effort of obtaining EMR data from HERON, while supporting external researchers. The analytics space offers a rich set of tools, services, and resources required by research. Within the protected environment, Green HERON users are provided the ability to select analytic tools such as R, SAS, and Python.

►
REDCap

REDCap is used by more than 700 institutions in over 60 countries and has become a dominant tool for electronic data capture for research studies at most academic medical centers in the United States. Clinical Informatics Services: Research Informatics provides consultation and build services within the Epic O2 electronic health record (EHR) to support research study administration, research data capture, and recruitment via real-time messaging through the MyChart patient portal, reports using Reporting Workbench, or point-of-care alerts.

►
Cerner Learning Health Network

The Learning Health Network is a large deidentified data resource with electronic health record data from over 100 million patients combined from multiple institutions, including our own. Most of the data come from institutions on Cerner, but they have the capability to harmonize in Epic institutions as well. Research Informatics can work with researchers to curate datasets and perform analytics in the LHN environment. The LHN also provides opportunities for multi-site studies.

►
Epic Cosmos

Research Informatics provides access to Epic’s Cosmos database and data science tools with deidentified data from electronic health records for over 200 million patients from hospitals across the United States, including our own. Cosmos data provides a good representation of the US population when compared to the United States Census. Research Informatics provides staff who are certified to use the Cosmos data science tools to help researchers take advantage of this powerful dataset.

►
SlicerDicer

SlicerDicer is a visual tool for exploring electronic health records at the UKHS. It includes powerful data exploration abilities for clinical, access, and revenue subject areas. In SlicerDicer, users can investigate a hunch and then refine their searches on the fly. Clinical researchers can examine trends and develop hypotheses by quickly explore large quantities of data.

►
Best Practice Advisory (BPAs)

BPAs provide targeted, patient-specific clinical guidance on a wide variety of topics. BPAs scan the entire patient record and can display notifications to physicians based on many key pieces of clinical data, such as lab results, assessment data, current medications, diagnoses, and histories. Research BPAs can alert a physician that the patient they are seeing may qualify for a study.

►
Greater Plains Collaborative (GPC)

GPC is a network of 12 leading medical centers in 9 states committed to a shared vision of improving healthcare delivery through ongoing learning, adoption of evidence-based practices, and active research dissemination. The GPC builds on strong research programs at our sites, existing community engagement and informatics infrastructures and data warehouses developed through the NIH CTSA initiative at most of our sites, extensive expertise with commercial EHR systems and terminology standardization, and strong working relationships between investigators and healthcare system information technology departments. Our network brings together a varied population with millions of patients across 1,550 miles covering 9 states.

►
Automated Cohort Discovery & Prescreening through Reporting Workbench

The Workbench is built directly in EPIC/O2. Research Informatics can create reports that identify patients who meet criteria and that can be refreshed by study coordinators. Studies with HIPAA waivers can use this to retrieve patient contact information for recruitment.

►
National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C)

The N3C is a partnership among the NCATS-supported Clinical Translational Science Awards (CTSA) Program hubs, the National Center for Data to Health (CD2H), and NIGMS-supported Institution Development Award Networks for Clinical and Translational Research (IDeA-CTR), with overall stewardship by NCATS. As a partner, KUMC is contributing COVID-19 clinical data to the N3C data enclave. KUMC researchers can request access to the N3C data enclave to conduct studies for answering critical COVID-19 related research questions.

►
Consortium for Clinical Characterization of COVID-19 by HER (4CE)

The 4CE is an international consortium for EHR data-driven studies of the COVID-19 pandemic. The goal of this effort is to inform doctors, epidemiologists, and the public about COVID-19 patients with data acquired through the healthcare process. 4CE is using a distributing learning framework where researchers post their queries through the coordinating center for participating sites to run the queries locally without raw EHR data leaving their institutions.

►
ResearchMatch

ResearchMatch is a nonprofit program funded by the National Institutes of Health (NIH). It helps to connect people interested in research studies with researchers from top medical centers across the U.S. The Office of the Chief Research Informatics Officer can connect researchers to the appropriate liaison at our institution.

►
Computing Resources

KUMC has a state-of-the-art-information technology infrastructure, which is connected to the other KU campuses throughout the State and is available both on and off campus. Students and faculty have access to the many computer labs located throughout the campus, which are equipped with scanners, HP laser printers, and Pentium 100 desktop PCs. Video support is also available through Information Resources and Institution Services. This resource service provides interactive television resources, including auditorium audio and video systems, slide to video converters, video playback, and closed-circuit television systems to rooms, ranging from an 8-seat conference room up to three 148-seat auditoriums and three 60-seat seminar rooms. This technology allows the rooms to communicate through the statewide video network, as well as up to three non-network sites inside and outside the Kansas borders. All computers on campus are connected to a 100 Megabit per second local area network that provides adequate network file storage. Networked file servers provide constant hardware backups of stored data through mirrored storage systems and daily tape backups are also performed. Weekly backups are stored off site for additional protection of research data. The network is managed by KUMC’s Information Resources who provides installation, training, and maintenance on all information systems. Local area networks are connected to a switched, 10 Gigabit Ethernet backbones that provides high speed Internet access through the KUMC Internet-2 communication network.

Office of Civil Rights & Title IX (OCRTIX) | v2025.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Lauren Jones McKown

KU Medical Center is committed to creating a sense of belonging where everyone feels comfortable to be themselves.in our programs for students, future students, staff, faculty, and patients. KU Medical Center centralizes broad efforts for recruitment and retention of faculty and senior administrative staff through four units—the Office of Civil Rights & Title IX (OCRTIX); the Equal Opportunity and Academic Compliance Office; the Office of International Programs; and the Office of Human Resources. Together, these Offices offer several programs to enhance our culture of belonging, Best Practices in Hiring, mandatory equal opportunity and harassment prevention, among others. The OCRTIX is a One University office led by the Associate Vice Chancellor for Civil Rights & Title IX and supported by an Assistant Vice Chancellor and 20 staff members, including 5 who primarily serve the Medical Center. The OCRTIX supports the Impact & Belonging Cabinet, a catalyst to drive advancement of constructive initiatives.

►
Office of Integrity & Compliance | v2025.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Natalie Holick

The major responsibility of the Office of Integrity & Compliance (OIC) is to ensure the highest standards of excellence and integrity in all research endeavors, and to promote ethical conduct of research through proactive mechanisms such as education and outreach; established policies and procedures for institutional and individual accountability; assessment, monitoring, auditing, and reporting; and institutional oversight committees. OIC administers KU Medical Center’s Conflicts of Interest Program as well as its Research Integrity Program in furtherance of the University’s commitment to scientific objectivity and the safety of our research participants. Additionally, OIC upholds KU Medical Center’s commitment to affirmative action by overseeing efforts to eliminate barriers and advance employment opportunities for individuals with disabilities and protected veterans.

KU Medical Center is committed to creating a welcoming environment where everyone feels valued and respected. The University recognizes that the achievements, skills, and experiences of everyone in our campus community are critical to the excellence of our research and academic programs. By fostering open communication and encouraging collaboration, KU Medical Center works to ensure that everyone has the opportunity to contribute meaningfully. Additionally, several University units, including Impact & Belonging, Integrity & Compliance, Civil Rights & Title IX, International Programs, and Human Resources, offer many professional development opportunities to cultivate environments in which all individuals can participate to the full extent of their capabilities, realize their aspirations, and best contribute their talents.

►
Human Research Protection Program (HRPP) | v2024.05 | Point(s) of Contact: Kyle Stephens

KUMC engages in research involving human subjects. A comprehensive Human Research Protection Program (HRPP) was developed to ensure the rights, safety and welfare of all participants recruited and/or enrolled in research projects by incorporating the principles found in the Belmont Report, specifically the three key concepts: respect for people, beneficence, and justice. All human subjects research conducted by KUMC faculty, students, and staff fall under the purview of the HRPP regardless of funding source and regardless of research location.

The purpose of the HRPP is to monitor, evaluate, and improve the protections of human research participants. The program oversees the institutional review process related to ethical and regulatory considerations, conflicts of interest, quality assurance, privacy, and safety. The HRPP is responsible for ensuring that all personnel involved in research activities understand and comply with the ethical standards and regulatory requirements governing all aspects of human research.

KUMC has a Federalwide Assurance (FWA) outlining policies implementing federal regulations. This assurance applies to all projects that are federally funded or supported and must comply with federal regulations (OHRP/DHHS or FDA, etc). The HRPP has authority to approve, require modifications in (to secure approval), or disapprove research involving human subjects.

Since 2007, KUMC has been accredited by the Association for the Accreditation of Human Research Protection Programs (AAHRPP), an independent, non-profit accrediting body. AAHRPP promotes high-quality research through an accreditation process that helps organizations worldwide strengthen their HRPPs. KUMC accreditation was most recently renewed in 2025.

►
Institutional Animal Care & Use Committee | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Nathan Culley

The KUMC Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) is administered by the Office of Regulatory Affairs for Biological Sciences. KUMC’s animal care program provides regulatory and ethical guidance for the KUMC research community, IACUC administrative support, protocol development and pre-review services to the research community, compliance monitoring of the animal care and use program, and training and resources for the KUMC research community.

KUMC is fully accredited by the Association for the Assessment of Accreditation of Laboratory Animal Care, International (AAALAC), which requires adherence to the highest standards of animal care and use by accredited institutions. The accreditation, which is entirely voluntary, has been continuous since 1996. In addition, KUMC is registered as a research facility with the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) and KUMC also holds a Category I Assurance with the Public Health Service (through the NIH's Office of Laboratory Animal Welfare).
