Information Technology | v2024.05 | Point(s) of Contact: Jeremy Pennington

The KUMC Information Technology (IT) department provides centralized IT services for the KUMC campus. An IT Service Catalog details about 70 standard services. For more complex problems and unique needs not specifically addressed in the IT Service Catalog, business analysis and project management are available through the Enterprise Project Management Office (EPMO).

Secure file storage is provided for individuals and departments, as well as for research projects with sensitive and high-risk data. Centrally stored data is routinely backed up to and synchronized with an offsite location. Our campus network includes wireless (802.11g - 802.11ac) connectivity and wired gigabit connectivity to the desktop. The approximate 35 campus buildings are redundantly connected over a 40-gigabit aggregate network backbone. The network is connected to Internet and Internet2 though a redundant 20-gigabit connection. Custom application and web development are also available, which includes data and systems integration. Complete computer lifecycle support is provided from procurement, support, and upgrades through secure disposal. Current campus communication and collaboration tools include email, phone conferencing, web conferencing, video conferencing, document imaging, and large/secure file transfer, along with Viva Engage, SharePoint, Microsoft Teams, and Zoom. High performance computing is accessible to KUMC through the KU main campus in Lawrence.

KUMC Information Technology provides researchers and faculty with critical technology infrastructure, as well as technical services and support. To continue to address research needs for large amounts of reliable storage, KUMC funded a $2.5M Research and Employee File-Level Storage Expansion, providing long-term storage via expandable two-petabyte NAS with redundant systems at offsite locations.

Multifactor authorization (MFA) is enabled for all high-risk data systems to further protect KUMC research and financial data from compromised accounts, e.g., phishing. With our Kiteworks Secure File Transfer service, researchers can securely send and receive large files from colleagues at KUMC and/or external recipients. Mimecast secure email is an encrypted messaging system that works seamlessly with the Medical Center's existing email system. Mimecast can encrypt email as it leaves KUMC private networks and heads out onto the Internet to further reduce SPAM e-mail messages, virus attachments, and phishing attacks aimed at compromising our researchers.

KUMC continues its implementation of Microsoft 365 allowing faculty, staff and students the ability to collaborate and share data not classified as Restricted with external collaborators. All email accounts are now in Exchange online and work continues to evaluate and securely allow other collaboration tools within Microsoft 365 to provide researchers and their teams a more advanced and better integrated Office platform. KUMC SharePoint is a browser-based collaboration platform that includes document management and workflow management.

Researchers can securely collaborate in real-time with web (Microsoft Teams and Zoom) conferencing. KUMC Library staff supports researchers and research administrators with NIH public access requirements, including consultations, training, troubleshooting manuscript submissions, and reporting. IT policies and procedures are reviewed and updated annually to ensure our research mission is well protected and remains competitive in the marketplace.

KU Innovation Park | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Emily Miller

KU Innovation Park is an independent, non-profit economic development organization dedicated to a growing community of innovation, entrepreneurship, and commercialization. The Park offers a variety of enterprise services for technology and bioscience businesses at any level, from concept to industry. Across its facilities the Park offers lab and office space, as well as a range of shared workspaces to meet the needs of companies at all stages of growth. More than a physical location, the Park is a regional ecosystem of facilities, services, people, and partners dedicated to creating more diverse, resilient, and equitable Kansas economy. With the support of its underlying coalition of public and private stakeholders, and alongside its vast network of community, industry, and government partners, the Park seeks to leverage our region’s existing strengths and assets to build the high-growth, innovation-focused industry clusters that will drive Kansas’ long-term economic growth, sustainability, and prosperity for decades to come.

The Park and its founding stakeholders work closely with the University to maximize its economic development potential and help retain its skilled graduates in the region. For private industry firms interested in engaging in collaborative research with the University, utilizing university facilities and intellectual property, or accessing its pipeline of skilled students and graduates the Park serves as a gateway to the University and an opportunity to operate in highly specialized, privately-owned facilities located directly adjacent to campus.

The University of Kansas Center for Technology Commercialization (KUCTC) | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: KUCTC Staff

KUCTC manages all KU’s intellectual property, brings KU’s innovations to the marketplace, and partners with industry on licensing technologies. KUCTC works across the entire KU research ecosystem to identify, review, and protect intellectual property resulting from research. The center negotiates licenses for KU’s intellectual property and collaborates with innovation partners to support startup endeavors and industry engagement. In addition, KUCTC ensures licensee compliance and distribution of revenues according to policy. KUCTC serves all of KU in additional ways by educating the research community on commercialization and intellectual property, marketing KU’s intellectual property, and partnering with other KU organizations to assist in accelerating technology development and new venture creation.

The University of Kansas Libraries | v2025.01 | Point(s) of Contact: Erich Kessler, Kent Miller

One of the top 50 libraries in the Association of Research Libraries, KU Libraries consists of seven main campus locations along with the A. R. Dykes Library of the Health Sciences on the University of Kansas Medical Center campus in Kansas City, Kansas. Additionally, the Kansas City campus includes the Clendening History of Medicine Library and Museum. The School of Medicine in Wichita, Kansas contains the Farha Medical Library. With our resources and expertise, KU/KUMC Libraries work to advance discovery, innovation and learning for our faculty, staff, students as well as the state and a rapidly expanding community of world scholars. The A.R. Dykes library participates in the grant funded Network of National Libraries of Medicine program to recruit and manage a biomedical librarian whose mission is to provide health information education and outreach services to patrons and entities throughout the state of Kansas as well as nationwide. KU/KUMC libraries are leaders in the Open Access movement. KU was the first public institution in the U.S. to adopt a faculty-led open access policy and was a founding member of the Coalition of Open Access Policy institutions. KUMC biomedical librarians provide research and instruction to our faculty, staff and students in the form of classroom instruction, research guides, individual and group consultations and by conducting systematic reviews with faculty. Biomedical librarians are available via a calendar scheduling service, Instant Messaging, email, phone and in-person. The medical libraries provide student-friendly study spaces with a variety of seating and standing study areas. A wide range of electronic information resources are available to all KUMC faculty, staff and students on all campuses and can be accessed remotely from anywhere with a KUMC login. Interlibrary loan services provide our users with books and journal articles not available within our campus collections. A full description of the A.R. Dykes Library mission and services can be found on our website: https://www.kumc.edu/dykes-library.html

The University of Kansas Health System | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Emily Miller

The University of Kansas Health System is one of the nation’s leading health systems, operating more than 140 hospital and clinic locations across the region. On its main campus, located in Kansas City, Kansas, The University of Kansas Hospital has ranked among the top hospitals in the country every year since 2007. The hospital is a nationally verified Level 1 Trauma Center and the only hospital in the region to have any medical and surgical adult specialties that ranked among the top 50 nationwide. The health system is equipped with more than 1,200 staffed beds. In 2024, the heath system provided high-quality care during 133,000 emergency visits and 1.7 million outpatient visits, offering a variety of specialized treatments to provide comprehensive care to its patients. Among the specialized services are those offered through the Center for Advanced Heart Care, the Mid America Radiation Center, the KU Cancer Center, the Bloch Cancer Care Pavilion, the Asher Comprehensive Spine Center, the Burnett Burn Center, the Sutherland Institute, the Epilepsy Center, the Diabetes Education and Research Center, the Senior Citizens Health Center, the Family Practice Clinic, and other sites within the hospital.

Physician practices represent more than 200 specialty areas, including kidney transplant surgery, renal dialysis, treatment of polycystic kidney disease, the only liver transplant program in the region, sterile environments for bone marrow transplant patients and other patients whose immune systems are not functioning properly, a state-of-the art facility for delicate facial and body reconstruction surgery services, hyperbaric oxygen therapy, comprehensive cardiology care, arthritis clinics with immunology specialists, medical and surgical treatments for epilepsy, specialized neurology programs for the treatment of multiple sclerosis and headaches as well as Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, and comprehensive gynecologic and obstetrics services for problem pregnancies with an intensive care nursery for premature and sick newborns. Additionally, comprehensive rehabilitation services and psychiatric services are offered on both an inpatient and outpatient basis.

Training Programs
►
Frontiers Scholars Club | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Nikki Nollen, Holly Zink

The Frontiers Scholars Club (FSC) offers a structured, interdisciplinary monthly meeting for scholars and trainees across the Frontiers partner organizations conducting clinical and translational research. It serves as a platform for interactive networking, professional development, and training seminars facilitated by senior researchers. The FSC also provides a collaborative forum for predoctoral students, postdoctoral trainees, and junior faculty to present their research to peers and receive constructive feedback. Each meeting is designed to enhance core clinical and translational research competencies, including informatics, mentorship, manuscript and grant writing, IRB processes, and general career development. The FSC fosters a supportive research community and helps junior researchers develop essential skills for long-term success. Scholars from all disciplines and research phases at Frontiers-affiliated institutions are encouraged to apply for membership, as it offers a unique opportunity to grow and thrive in the field of clinical and translational research.

►
Kansas MD-PhD Physician Scientist Training Program | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Timothy Fields

The Kansas MD-PhD Physician Scientist Training Program (T32GM138077) will recruit, retain, and develop a diverse group of physician-scientists (MD-PhD) to become leaders in biomedical research and translational clinical practice. Short-term goals for MSTP-supported trainees include development of clinical, research, and communication skills, publication of research results, submission of predoctoral fellowship proposals, and timely progression to degrees. Long-term goals for training include participation in the biomedical workforce and success in obtaining extramural funding. We matriculate ~3-5 students annually from a pool of ~80-90 nation-wide applicants. Recent successful applicants have had an average of 20.7 months of research experience prior to matriculation. Our students have been recruited from schools in 21 states across the country, and, historically, our recruitment of female students and students from underrepresented groups has exceeded the national average for MD-PhD programs. Our graduates have successfully competed for residencies at top academic medical schools. Among our alumni who have entered the workforce are those with successful careers in industry, academia, and government. Our success is based on strategic pairing of candidates with NIH funded basic and clinical science mentors, the strong support from the institution and state, and the integrated training environment that we provide. Students have training opportunities with faculty in 17 departments/programs and 31 different Centers and Institutes, including the Cancer Center, the University of Kansas Clinical and Translational Science Institute (CTSI), and Alzheimer's Disease Center as well as with affiliated faculty at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research.

►
KL2 Scholars Program | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Nikki Nollen, Holly Zink

The KL2 Mentored Research Career Development Program selects and supports a talented group of junior scientists committed to advancing clinical and translational research. The NIH-funded KL2 Mentored Career Development Award provides protected research time, intensive mentorship, and specialized training to equip junior faculty with the skills necessary for independent research careers. Early in the program, scholars develop an Individual Development Plan (IDP) and assemble an interdisciplinary mentorship team tailored to their research and career goals. Scholars collaborate closely with mentors on all aspects of professional growth and engage with Frontiers resources and content experts to build research connections and interdisciplinary collaborations. KL2 Scholars receive comprehensive career development training through participation in the Frontiers Scholars Club (FSC), which offers targeted programming to support scholars during this pivotal transition to research independence, reassuring them about the resources available.

The purpose of the BRTP is to facilitate the development of externally funded individual pre- and post-doctoral fellowships, institutional training grants, and faculty research grants. The BRTP is an outgrowth of the Wesley Foundation/Kansas Health Foundation Training Program in Cancer Research that was established in 2000. Recognizing that this program led directly to increases in research productivity and external grant support, the Executive Vice Chancellor’s office invests over $200,000 in the program annually. Applicants to this competitive program submit fellowship-formatted applications that are reviewed by 2-3 KUMC faculty investigators in a meeting modeled after an NIH Study Section. Applicants receive feedback about their training and research plans that is critical for external applications. By simulating an NIH Study Section, the BRTP also provides junior faculty valuable experience reviewing proposals alongside senior faculty with more extensive NIH Study Section experience. Each year’s awardees present their research at an annual BRTP Symposium that includes an external keynote speaker. The BRTP is open to students from each of KUMC’s schools: Medicine, Health Professions, and Nursing.

Through research carried out at university centers like the CCHD, service delivery to children and adults with DD evolves into best practices, improving the quality of life for individuals, families, and communities.

The training program leverages resources and the KU ADRC's research strengths to create a developmental pathway for the next generation of ADRD basic, translational, and clinical scientists. Funding provides critical support to synergize with ongoing efforts, further enhance the ADRC's training efforts, and draw on the center's unique resources, exceptional mentors, supportive collaborators, and growing breadth of educational opportunities.

KUMC Shared Research Resources
►
Airway & Asthma Translational Research Unit | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Jonathan Boomer

The Airway & Asthma Translational Research Unit (AATRU) laboratory was established in 1995 to acquire, securely store, and use integrated human airway biospecimens and clinical data to better understand the biochemical, molecular, and transcriptional basis for the structural and physiological consequences of airway remodeling in lung diseases, specifically severe asthma. The laboratory goal is to advance understanding of the mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of asthma leading to new strategies for trial designs and therapeutic interventions. The AATRU focuses on understanding the origins of asthma and how to decrease asthma morbidity and mortality using translational methods. The AATRU group currently has >25 ongoing studies, all of which have opportunities for students, residents, fellows, and junior faculty to perform focused research in an area of interest.

►
Biospecimen Processing

The laboratory supports >25 clinical trials run at KUMC. Specimens are procured using standardized, validated procedures that allows clinical data to be referenced in coordination with structural, mechanistic as well as biochemical for genomic, metabolomic, proteomic, microbiome analyses in unraveling asthma endotypes.

AATRU also provides consultation and collaborative services to investigators wishing to study human airways. The AATRU laboratory is a BSL-2 facility that houses numerous clinical and research temperature-controlled centrifuges; two tissue culture rooms containing Class II biosafety cabinets and tissue culture incubators; long term storage units (-80°C and LN2 freezers), microscopes; computer workstations and barcode scanners; as well as bench top incubators and shakers. Adult and Pediatric biospecimens facilitate understanding the underlying pathophysiology of asthma endotypes. Biospecimens consist of study participant blood products, including serum, plasma, as well as peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs); urine, feces, induced and spontaneous sputum, nasal fluid and tissue, exhaled breath condensate (EBC), bronchial alveolar lavage fluid and endobronchial airway tissue and cells.

The laboratory supports biospecimen processing, aliquoting, storage, and shipping these specimens to trial centers and collaborators throughout the world. As part of Biospecimen processing, the laboratory has established an Airway Biobank which houses >850 unique participants and >3,500 biospecimens over the past 25+ years of human research.

►
Airway Biobank

AATRU Database: A REDCap based secure electronic database captures subject clinical data, run by Project Design and Analysis - Enterprise Sciences at KUMC. Clinical data consists of clinical laboratory data, medications, lung function testing, CT/MRI imaging as well as subject demographics enabling research to be undertaken on well characterized subject populations. AATRU Biospecimen Database: An electronic database built on open-source technology called Open Specimen run by the Research Institute of Technology Biostatistics and Data Science at KUMC. Open Specimen is a laboratory information system for cataloging, storage, and distribution of biospecimens for future and collaborative research.

►
Tissue Analysis: Morphometrics

Airway remodeling in lung diseases including asthma results in measurable quantitative alterations of the structure of the lung. A bronchoscopist uses a bronchoscope to visualize the airways and forceps to collect microscopic pieces of tissue. This tissue is fixed, embedded and sectioned then processed for Histology stains (H&E) or Immuno-histochemistry (IHC) procedures. Histology stains and IHC allow visualization of specific proteins using light microscopy. The stained or labeled sectioned tissue is captured on a Nikon Eclipse Ni-U tiling microscope as a colored image. This image is loaded into Image Analysis Software (Image Pro 10, Mediacy) for additional digital processing and measurement analysis. In severe asthma the epithelium and laminar reticularis thickens and an increase in smooth muscle mass is observed. In addition, the presence of goblet cells, using specific histology stains such as mucicarmine, can be identified in the epithelium which produce mucus as a pathological feature of asthma. This technique is one of the few recognized measures of airway remodeling in biopsy tissue. The laboratory has ongoing Image Analysis projects analyzing biopsy tissue from ongoing NIH funded studies including SARPIII and IV.

►
Cellular Analysis: Confocal Microscopy

Airway remodeling can be visualized at the cellular level using high-image resolution techniques like immunofluorescent confocal microscopy. Cellular markers including receptors, proteins, transcription factors and nuclei can be labeled with specific antibodies or dyes conjugated to a fluorophore with specific excitation and emission wavelengths. The fluorescent microscope captures these fluorophores in x-y and z planes to generate a 3D image. Images can be analyzed for co-localization of proteins, cell type specific identification and expression and can be reconstructed in a 3D space using Image Analysis Software (Image Pro 10) to recapitulate the cellular and sub-cellular architecture of the epithelium.

►
In Vitro Modeling: Air Liquid Interface

The AATRU takes advantage of an in vitro cell culture model that replicates the lung to perform mechanistic studies on airway epithelium to understand the endotypes of asthma and test novel biologics. Air liquid interface (ALI) cultures are when epithelial cells are isolated and cultured from endobronchial brushes obtained from the human airway. Epithelial cells are first expanded in submerged cultures then transferred to porous inserts until confluent. Once confluent, the apical fluid is removed exposing the epithelium to 'air', like the environment within the lung, and the basal medium is changed to induce epithelial cell differentiation. A pseudostratified epithelium contains the cell types that make up the airways – ciliated, basal as well as secretory and mucus producing cells after ~30 days of culture.

►
Biomarker Analysis: Flow Cytometry & ELISA

The laboratory goal is to advance understanding of the mechanisms underlying the pathophysiology of asthma leading to new strategies for trial designs and therapeutic interventions. The AATRU also pursues biomarker analysis to aid in determining the numerous endotypes of asthma as well as impacts of biologics on the patho-physiology of asthma. Therefore, the laboratory is setup to perform routine ELISAs or Multi-plex Arrays to identify and quantitate soluble proteins in serum, plasma, urine, BAL, and sputum. In addition, individual cells isolated from blood (PBMCs), BAL or sputum can be labeled for cell type identification, receptor profiling or intra-cellular proteins using wavelength specific fluorophore conjugated reagents run in a single-cell manner followed by multi-color analysis on individual cells using the KUMC Flow Cytometry Core Facility.

Analytical Core Laboratory | v2022.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Bruno Hagenbuch

The ACL was founded as a shared equipment laboratory (a Core laboratory) around 2008 as part of a Center for Biomedical Research Excellence (COBRE) grant awarded to the department of Pharmacology, Toxicology and Therapeutics in 2006. This COBRE grant was renewed for the third and final time in 2016 (P30GM118247).

The ACL maintains a varied instrument suite designed to assist KUMC's basic research community by providing access to the advanced instrumentation needed to examine toxicants, endogenous metabolites, biotherapeutic compounds and the products of their metabolic break-down. Stated more simply, the ACL's mission is to assist with the execution of quantitative analysis of small- or large (and intact) molecule biological analytes.

Instruments operated in the ACL are two qPCR instruments (BioRad CFX384 and StepOnePlus), two plate-readers (Synergy 2 and Tecan Infinite 200 Pro), a HORIBA FluoroMax-4 spectrophotometer and a gel-imager (LI-COR Odyssey XF) with image analysis software (ImageStudio Lite). These instruments make up the Pharmacology department's shared instrument suite. In addition, the ACL also hosts a Waters Xevo TQ-XS and a Waters Synapt HDMS mass spectrometer, and services using these instruments are available on a collaborative basis within KUMC. However, currently no mass spectrometry services are offered outside KUMC.

Bioinformatics is the computational analysis of biological information to enable the study of nucleic acid sequences, peptides, proteins, genes, and genomes using computer software and databases. The mission of this facility is to advance the understanding of integrative functions in biological systems, including human, through the application of computational models and data analysis with focus on Next Generation Sequencing Data Analysis and Microarray Data Analysis. The Biospecimen Repository Core Facility (BRCF) is an established biospecimen bank of the University of Kansas Cancer Center (KUCC) and the KU Medical Center that supports sample processing and storage for a wide variety of investigator-initiated studies on the KUMC campus. Biostatistics & Data Science | v2025.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Matt Mayo, Megan Tremblay

The mission of the Department of Biostatistics & Data Science is to provide an infrastructure of biostatistical, bioinformatics, informatics, and data science expertise to support and enhance the research, service, and educational needs of KUMC. There is approximately 7,000 ft2 of office space within the Department of Biostatistics & Data Science at University of Kansas Medical Center, which includes a conference room, various offices, equipment, and services such as computers, copiers, faxing, overnight mailing, and portable display cases. There are 26 Ph.D. Biostatistics Faculty, 7 M.S. Biostatisticians, 14 Informatics Specialists, 2 Project Managers, 2 Administrators, 1 Administrative Assistant. Our faculty members are active researchers collaborating and consulting in research projects and initiatives throughout the Medical Center, in addition to pursuit of their own research agendas and participation in curricular instruction. Expertise in the department includes linear, nonlinear, and longitudinal modeling, clinical trial and experimental design, survival analysis, categorical data analysis, robust statistics, psychometric methods, Bayesian methodology and statistical genomics. Our innovative MS and PhD programs were created to help meet the ever-increasing demand for biostatisticians needed to take leadership roles in careers as researchers and educators in academia, government and industry. The course work, seminars and collaborative research experience have been designed so that our graduates acquire the knowledge and expertise that allows them to work at the frontier of their field.

The Department of Biostatistics & Data Science has invested over $1M toward hardware since 2009 to enhance the informatics and biostatistical computing abilities. All computers in the Department of Biostatistics & Data Science are connected to a 10 Gigabyte per second local area network that provides more than 100 Terabytes of network file storage. Networked file servers offer continuous hardware backups of stored data through mirrored storage systems, along with daily tape backups. Weekly tape backups are stored off-site for additional protection of research data. The network is managed by KUMC’s Information Resources who provide installation, training, and maintenance on all information systems. The Department of Biostatistics & Data Science local area network is connected to a switched, 10 Gigabit Ethernet backbone that provides high-speed Internet access through the KUMC Internet2 communication network. Currently, KUMC’s Internet2 access is via the Kansas Research and Education Network (KanREN). KanREN supports Internet2 connectivity for all of its members via a 10Gbps link to the Great Plains Network (GPN), and KUMC is connected to KanREN via a 1 Gigabit per second connection. This high-speed network provides each workstation with access to the World Wide Web, electronic mail, electronic file transfer, and shared CD-ROM-based databases.

►
Hardware

The Department of Biostatistics & Data Science maintains:

  • Statistical analysis server with 24 Xeon CPU cores at 3.6 GHz with 64 GB of memory, 15 TB of available hard drive space, D2D4004 dynamic de-duplication backup device, LTO-4 Ultrium 1760 tape backup system
  • Shared high speed workstation with dual Xeon 3.6 GHz processors, 32GB of SDRAM, >800GB of highspeed storage, digital tape backup, DVD read/write optical drive
►
Statistical & Mathematical Software

Software available includes WinBUGS/OpenBUGS, R, Mplus, MATLAB, SAS, SPSS, and MSOffice™, Minitab, S-PLUS, LogXact, StatXact, EGRET, SOLAS, WinNonlin, nQuery, Mathematica, Mathcad, DIGITAL Visual Fortran Professional, DBMSCopy, SigmaPlot, Access, MS SQL, OmniForm, Oracle, Tableau, MATLAB, JMP, SAS, SPSS, STATA, IPA and Resampling Stats. WinNonlin, Nquery, Mathcad, SigmaPlot, Excel, Access, MySQL, Oracle, PLSQL, MS Visual Studio, SQL server, Postgresql, RStudio, Shinyr. Computer resources primarily consist of Windows 10 connected to a centralized Authentication system.

►
Security

The network is protected by a firewall and all computers are password protected. All network data are backed up nightly and stored in a secure off-site location. All individuals are required to undergo annual computer security training. Yet another level of security is conveyed by the fact that the building in which the key personnel are located has limited electronic passkey access during non-business hours i.e., between 6 pm - 6 am and 24 hrs during weekends and national holidays. In addition, access to the data centers is severely restricted requiring an electronic passkey or a physical key. Individually identifiable or deducible data will not be transmitted by unsecured telecommunications, which include the Internet, email, and electronic File Transfer Protocol. Further, the data will not be physically moved or transmitted in any way from its location without written approval from appropriate personnel. Finally, all output containing individual identifiable information is treated as confidential data. This information is never transferred electronically via email or other protocols. Shredders are used on any printed material containing individual identifiers.

►
CRIS Servers

There are eight virtualized Windows Servers dedicated to supporting CRIS (Comprehensive Research Information System managed by Information Resources). The database server is an Intel ® Xeon ® CPU L5420 @ 2.67 GHz, 3.00 GHz, 24.00 GB of RAM; with Microsoft Windows Server 2016 OS. It is backed up daily using SyncSort's Backup Express. The application server is an Intel ® Xeon ® CPU L5420 @ 2.50 GHz, 3.00 GHz, 24.00 GB of RAM, with Microsoft Windows Server 2016 OS. It is backed up daily using SyncSort's Backup Express. Four similar virtualized servers are used for development and testing purposes.

►
Curated Cancer Clinical Outcomes Database (C3OD)

Data used to determine patient eligibility for cancer clinical trials often come from disparate sources that are typically maintained by different groups within an institution, use differing technologies, and are stored in different formats. Collecting data and resolving inconsistencies across sources increase the time it takes to screen eligible patients, potentially delaying study completion. To address these challenges, the Biostatistics and Informatics Shared Resource at The University of Kansas Cancer Center developed the Curated Cancer Clinical Outcomes Database (C3OD). C3OD merges data from the electronic medical record, tumor registry, biospecimen and data registry, and allows querying through a single unified platform. By centralizing access and maintaining appropriate controls, C3OD allows researchers to obtain detailed information more rapidly about each patient to accelerate eligibility screening.

►
Velos eResearch (aka CRIS Comprehensive Research Information System

Velos supports patient recruitment, patient scheduling, study monitoring, project planning, study design, protocol compliance, budget, invoicing, and milestone management, data safety monitoring, adverse event reporting, system integration and study execution. Velos supports both study administration and clinical data management. This type of design is fundamental to Velos’ customer service abilities to solve customers’ research, information, and coordination challenges. Velos already has dozens of working laboratory, medical record, and device interfaces that are already in production; Compliance with industry standards (such as CFR11) and a commitment to supporting standards that foster higher collaboration. Velos is active in and supportive of government initiatives intended to foster greater collaboration among researchers (example FDA funded studies). Patient-level of study-level system architecture. Most research systems were primarily designed for research sponsors and focus on the needs of single studies. The system architecture to support research sites well is quite different and must consider both patient- and study-level views and integrate the two. Advanced technology and security features to support multi-institutional, cooperative trials, community-based research, and patient self-reporting, in a single environment. Through these capabilities, Velos helps effect a paradigm shift from the current sponsor centric clinical research information model to one that is investigator centric. In doing so, Velos believes it can help its customers, and the research community in general, unleash tremendous improvements in research productivity, collaboration, and, ultimately, patient care.

►
OpenSpecimen

OpenSpecimen is an integrated biobank management software. Which serves as a cost-effective solution to maintain specimen inventory and data related to those specimens for a large biobanks and lab activities. Under a single roof Inventory for large biorepository protocol or by a lab with many smaller projects is banked. If utilized by multiple departments/sites within one institution, specimens can be transferred within the system from one group to the next to maintain a tracking log of all destinations/freezer locations. Departments can track all biospecimens from collection to utilization for prospective biobanking, longitudinal collections, multisite clinical studies, or non-human collections. It also supports clinical and pathology data collection based on the study or disease (e.g., smoking history, pathological annotations, genetics and genomic testing information, standard laboratory test results, etc.) along with a robust reporting module.

►
Accrual Prediction Application

Monitoring subject recruitment is key to the success of a clinical trial. Accordingly, researchers have developed accrual-monitoring tools to support the design and conduct of trials. At an institutional level, delays in identifying studies with high risk of accrual failure can lead to inefficient and costly trials with little chances of meeting study objectives. First released in 2016, the Accrual Prediction Program summarizes enrollment information for active studies categorized by various trial attributes. The web application supports real-time evidence-based decision making for strategic resource allocation and study management of over 120 ongoing clinical trials at the University of Kansas Cancer Center.

►
Data Analytics

For reporting and dashboard creation purposes we utilize shiny or Tableau that makes it easy to build interactive web application using R and Tableau Desktop correspondingly. Our intention of utilizing these platforms is to allow users to ask questions rather than learning a software, with built in visual best practices and limitless data exploration.

Rodent Surgical Services

Genetic models of rodent disease are often generated at the request of a PI in coordination with the Transgenic and Stem Cell Core followed by behavioral testing of rodents in the Rodent Behavior Facilities. For non-genetic disease models, the process often begins with DMA’s Rodent Surgical Services. Disease Model and Assessment Services staff are proficient in several surgical techniques such as ovariectomy, cortical impact, stereotactic surgery, venipuncture, TBI, and SCI. These services are provided through Core facilities consisting of two fully equipped surgical suites. Shared procedure suites for rodent surgery, or other non-surgical procedures are in 2023 and 2031 HLSIC. These suites are fully equipped with stereomicroscope, warming bed, cautery, anesthesia, and more. The equipment and space are scheduled and maintained by DMA staff. Each facility contains electrocautery, warming pads, inhalational anesthesia regulators, rodent ventilators, and Nikon stereomicroscopes, some of which are equipped with digital color cameras and computers for capturing microsurgical procedures. Physiological assessment facilities housed in HLSIC 2031 include instrumentation for measuring a variety of physiological parameters including blood pressure and heart rate from awake rodents (Coda 6 non-invasive BP monitor from Kent Scientific); nerve conduction, EMG, single fiber, and motor unit analysis (Viasys); regional blood flow (Oxyflow Laser Doppler Flowmetry), cardiovascular function, force, pressure, etc. (PowerLab 8 channel high performance data acquisition systems with computers). Additional equipment includes stimulators, syringe infusion pumps, low-noise rodent heating controllers, end tidal CO2 analyzer, and rodent ventilators.

►
Shared Equipment Services

Shared-equipment room 2015 HLSIC houses common molecular biology equipment such as shaking and non-shaking incubators, centrifuges, plate readers, plate washers, -80°C freezers, a state- of- the- art gel imaging system, the Blitz and Octet biolayer interferometers, and more. Scientific equipment includes Victor3 and SpectraMax M5 plate readers, a Wellwash AC automated plate washing system, Varian UV-visible spectrophotometer, Bio-Rad ChemiDoc and Molecular Imager Plus gel imagers, Innova 44 Incubator/Shakers (2), a ThermoElectron SpeedGel Dryer, Osmette III osmometer, a BioRad Gene Pulser Xcell, a ThermoElectron Corp RC-6 plus high-speed centrifuge, two large -80oC Forma freezers, Beckman Airfuge and ultracentrifuge, ovens and miscellaneous lab equipment. The RBF/DMA maintain the latest versions of common software programs including those by Microsoft, Adobe, SPSS, Dreamweaver, and Creative Suite for installation on licensed workstations. The DMA has access to six desktop and laptop computers, as well as an array of printers, storage and backup media and cloud systems, scanners, and other general use computer equipment. Diagnostic and computer maintenance software includes Partition Magic, Norton Utilities, Norton System Works, Tech Tools Pro, and Drive for Macintosh.

►
Immunoassay Services

Disease Model and Assessment Services offers a wide range of ELISA-based immunoassay analysis services. Samples from rodents or humans can be tested for research or clinical biomarkers of disease. Currently, investigators can request the assays of interest based on commercial availability. The most well utilized assays include insulin, c-peptide, cotinine, IL-6, TNF-α, vitamin D, cortisol, amylin, and IGF-1. These assays are very popular and are often ideal for projects that need large-scale, on-demand assays that do not require clinical laboratory assurances, thus lowering the costs to investigators substantially. Immunoassay services are provided through shared equipment resources maintained by DMA staff which includes a plate reader, shaking incubators, centrifuges, spectrophotometers and more. Luminex multi-analyte assays are offered in collaboration with the flowcytometry core.

►
Rodent Behavioral Testing

A key component of the DMA is the KUMC Rodent Behavior Facility (RBF). The mission of the RBF is to assist researchers in incorporating behavioral research techniques using rodents in their individual research projects. The KUMC RBF provides both equipment and services and is available for use following appropriate training and approval. RBF staff members are available to help design, execute and analyze behavioral experiments. Disease Model and Assessment Services personnel maintain and staff two distinct facilities that house an extensive array of behavioral testing equipment in approximately 1,500 ft2 of space specialized for testing of rodent cognitive, sensory, and motor function. They hold more than $750,000 in equipment for rodent behavioral testing equipment and software. Access to the facility is restricted to approved, trained personnel, and access is facilitated and coordinated via monitored online scheduling.

Rodent Behavior Facility equipment is located in two distinct facilities, one in each vivarium. The Hemenway RBF occupies G047 and G049 HLSIC, for a total of approximately 750 ft2. The RSF vivarium houses an additional 1,000 ft2 of rodent behavior space in 3005 RSF. Maintenance of two distinct testing locations allows investigators to follow LAR animal movement criteria to reduce pathogen contamination. Also, preservation of two testing facilities allows for increased throughput and utilization by multiple laboratories. Rodent behavioral testing equipment includes an array of Coulbourn Tru-Scan Activity Arenas for small rodents (mice, juvenile rats) and larger rodents (adult rats) for automated analysis of rodent locomotor activities; Two BASi Force-Plate Actimeters and several force-plate actometers (fabricated by a KIDDRC patent holder member) of assorted sizes for locomotor assessment; a mouse social interaction arena; Rota-Rod stations for rats and mice; and six startle-reflex chambers (Kinder Scientific). Sensory testing equipment includes Hot- and cold-Plate Thermal Analgesiometers, a Randall-Sellito deep sensitivity testing system; two sets of Semmes- Weinstein Monofilaments, one electronic Von Frey system, and two Thermal Paw Analgesiometers (UCSD), meal pattern analysis systems, inclined hanging screens, inclined planes, balance beams, grid walk platforms, elevated plus mazes (rat and mouse sized), a radial arm water maze and Morris water maze, forced swim; conditioned fear equipment, one grip strength system, several Y-mazes and one large modifiable multiple-T maze; a DigiGait Imaging system; MiniMitter Telemetry system; fourteen small and two large sound-attenuating chambers for housing testing equipment, thus providing testing free of noise distractions. The RBF also maintains two small digital video cameras, several web-linked webcams, and two infrared illumination lamps to provide flexible video monitoring and/or recording in ambient or low-light conditions. Noldus tracking software and camera systems are available for automated data collection in many of the open-arena type behavioral assays.

►
ACUP Preparation, data acquisition & statistical analysis

DMA Services maintains IACUC-approved text for many of the surgical, behavioral, and metabolic services supported by the Core. Investigators can utilize this approved text to streamline incorporation of new testing strategies into their experimental design. DMA staff partners with the Office of Regulatory Affairs for Biological Sciences to maintain up-to-date procedural text for behavioral and metabolic testing within the ACUP submission tool and readily available to all PIs as needed.

In addition to the model development and phenotyping services offered through DMA Services staff, assistance with the experimental design and data analysis and presentation of rodent phenotyping experiments is supported through DMA Services. Data acquisition and statistical analyses, as well as assistance with data interpretation and presentation can be assisted by support from DMA Services staff members or the scientific director.

►
Electron Microscopy Core | v2026.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Bret Freudenthal, Ava Hammons

The Electron Microscopy Core (EMC) is equipped to support research projects using traditional Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM), and Cryogenic Electron Microscopy (cryo-EM). The core is equipped with a JEOL JEM-1400 TEM, Hitachi S-2700 SEM, TFS Glacios cryo-EM, TwoMP Mass Photometer, and ancillary equipment required for sample preparation, storage, and data analysis. In addition, experienced research personnel are available to assist investigators from experimental design to manuscript preparation. Full-service sample preparation and data collection options are also available. In addition, the EMC provides new users with training in both a 1:1 and a small group workshop format to support their independent usage of the facilities.

The EMC services include:

  • Negative stain, chemical fixation, resin infiltration, thin and thick sectioning, sample dehydration, and mounting for TEM or SEM applications.
  • Plunge freezing, grid clipping, mass photometry, data collection, analysis cluster utilization.
  • Single particle analysis utilizing the Glacios capabilities and personnel expertise.
►
Exercise & Human Performance, Metabolic & Body Composition Laboratories | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Ashley Herda

The Exercise and Human Performance and Metabolic and Body Composition Laboratories are part of the Department of Health, Sport, and Exercise Sciences in the School of Education and Human Sciences at the KU Edwards Campus (approximately 17 miles from KUMC’s main campus in Overland Park, Kansas). The Exercise and Human Performance Lab is dedicated to advancing knowledge in human performance through applied research and hands-on student learning. The lab focuses on evaluating the effects of various training programs on muscular strength and functional performance across the lifespan. In collaboration with the Metabolic and Body Composition Lab, it supports research on how exercise, aging, injury, and nutrition affect muscle and body composition. The lab is equipped to conduct complex resistance and aerobic training interventions and assess a wide range of physiological metrics, including:

  • Maximal strength and functional ability
  • Body and muscle composition
  • Resting metabolism and respiratory function
  • Maximal oxygen and energy consumption

Collectively, these labs work in synergy to create optimal evaluation of human interaction with exercise or nutritional interventions. https://edwardscampus.ku.edu/exercise-science-laboratories

►
Flow Cytometry Core Laboratory | v2025.04 | Point(s) of Contact: Mary Markiewicz, Richard Hastings

The KUMC flow cytometry core is equipped with the following flow cytometers:

  • 5 Laser (UV, Violet, Blue, Yellow-green, and Red) Cytek Aurora Spectral Analyzer
  • 5 Laser (UV, Violet, Blue, Yellow-green, and Red) Cytek Aurora Spectral Cell Sorter
  • 4 Laser (Violet, Blue, Yellow-green, and Red) Becton Dickinson FACSAria IIIu Cell Sorter
  • 3 Laser (Blue, Yellow-green, and Red) ThermoFisher Attune Analyzer

The core has licenses for the following flow cytometry analysis software packages:

  • Cytek SpectroFlo
  • Becton Dickinson FlowJo
  • De Novo FCS Express

The core is staffed by two FTE that can assist users with cell sorting, data acquisition, instrument training, and data analysis.

►
Frontiers Clinical & Translational Science Units | v2025.01 | Point(s) of Contact: Shelby Williams

The University of Kansas Clinical and Translational Science Institute (CTSI, simply called “Frontiers”) was established in 2007 to improve the health of Kansans by creating a novel and transformative translational research enterprise that spans bench to bedside to community. Frontiers represents an academic home with innovative training programs for clinical and translational investigators and provides an enhanced, coordinated translational research infrastructure. Additionally, in 2008, local county voters approved a dedicated sales tax, in perpetuity, which generates over $5 million annually to support clinical research and funds the KU Clinical Research Center. Frontiers was KU’s response to the NCATS Clinical and Translational Science Award (CTSA) initiative, was initially funded in 2011, and renewed for 5 additional years in 2017 and in 2021. The CTSI MPIs are Drs. Mario Castro and Steven Leeder. The CTSI Center for the Improvement of Mentored Experiences in Research (CIMER), adapted from the University of Wisconsin-Madison initiative led by Christine Pfund, was launched in early 2024 targeting faculty leadership of training programs, graduate programs, and department chairs.

►
Clinical & Translational Science Units (CTSUs)

Frontiers is committed to providing investigators with the state-of-the-art clinical facilities needed to accelerate clinical and translational research. The Clinical and Translational Science Units (CTSUs) provide comfortable, accessible space for participants and the support investigators and study teams need to successfully conduct clinical research. Staffed by experienced research personnel - including registered nurses, medical assistants, exercise physiologists, respiratory technicians, nurse practitioners and physicians – each Frontiers CTSU serves as a liaison for study teams as well as a resource when it comes to managing clinical research obstacles. CTSUs are available in the Kansas City Region and in Wichita, Kansas, to serve rural needs. Each CTSU is available to investigators from all Frontiers partner institutions. The CTSUs operate under a fee-for-service business model that supports growth and investment in CTR. CTSU staff work individually with investigators and study teams to build quotes specific to their study protocols. The CTSUs at KUMC, CMKC and KU-Wichita have been operational for nearly a decade and are showing steady increase in participant visit numbers. In fact, to address the growing demand on the Fairway unit, a second CTSU (Rainbow) was established on the KU medical campus in 2020. Finally, CTSU Swope was established in Kansas City, Missouri, to facilitate clinical research for investigators and their study teams in a location that serves the community and diverse populations.

►
CTSU Fairway

CTSU Fairway is in the suburban community of Fairway, Kansas, ~3 miles from the main KUMC campus. This state-of-the-art facility is staffed by experienced research nurses and medical assistants who support complex protocol procedures and record research data on CTSU generated resource documents/flow sheets. The facility includes clinical space, a sample processing lab (CLIA waived) to conduct point-of-care tests, research infusion unit, and exercise physiology lab with exercise physiologists available to assist with study related testing. The clinical space features nine multi-purpose exam rooms for outpatient evaluations, two phlebotomy bays for blood draws, two isolation exam rooms, and five cognitive testing rooms tailored for specialized assessments. The facility includes eight workstations for visiting study staff, ample storage for study-specific equipment and supplies, and a commercial-quality metabolic kitchen to support research collaborations with the Department of Dietetics and Nutrition. The Nutrition unit of CTSU Fairway includes an 830 ft² metabolic kitchen and a 600 ft² demonstration kitchen. The metabolic kitchen is a fully equipped professional grade used to provide standardized meals required by study protocols. The demonstration kitchen, which contains seating for 24, is a fully equipped kitchen with installed cameras and audiovisual aids to provide high class cooking skills and nutrition education programming.

►
CTSU Rainbow

CTSU Rainbow is located on the main University of Kansas Medical Center campus in Kansas City, Kansas. The unit is staffed by experienced research nurses, medical assistants, and respiratory technicians who support complex protocol procedures and document data on CTSU generated resource documents/flow sheets. The location houses clinical space, CLIA waived sample processing unit with two labs to conduct point-of-care tests, research infusion unit with space for visiting investigators, pulmonary testing lab with a respiratory technician available to assist with study related tasks, and exercise physiology space. The clinical space includes 11 exam rooms for multi-purpose outpatient evaluations, with two rooms that can be utilized as procedure rooms. There is a quiet room that can serve as a cognitive testing room, along with two phlebotomy bays. The facility provides dedicated workrooms for visiting study staff, space for site monitor visits, and a conference room suitable for study initiation visits or larger meetings. Additional features include a research and education kitchen, a negative pressure room, and a storage area for study teams to securely store protocol-specific equipment and supplies.

►
CTSU Swope

CTSU Swope is located ~6 miles from the main KUMC campus and is designed to facilitate clinical research for investigators and their study teams in an urban core location that serves a diverse community. The 1,020 ft² clinical space includes one exam room, two flexible exam rooms, work areas for study teams, a lab, and an equipment and supply storage area.

►
CTSU Wichita

CTSU Wichita is located on KUMC’s Wichita campus, approximately 200 miles from KUMC Kansas City. CTSU Wichita is available to support clinical research investigators for studies on the Wichita campus. This involves assistance with study startup and operationalization, including administrative oversight and training of investigators and site staff.

►
Genomics Core | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Clark Bloomer

The University of Kansas Medical Center Genomics Core is affiliated with the Kansas Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities Research Center (KIDDRC) and Frontiers: Clinical and Translational Science Institute (CTSI). The Genomics Core provides centralized access to next generation sequencing (NGS), single cell sequencing, spatial transcriptomics and support services to advance research conducted by investigators of KUMC, KU, Kansas Regents Institutions and member institutions of Frontiers CTSI. The mission of the Genomics Core is to accelerate investigator research by performing large scale global NGS, single cell genomics, spatial expression, and epigenomic sequencing projects. To meet investigator’s research support requirements, the Genomics Core strives to enhance its genomics capabilities by maintaining the most advanced instrumentation and technologies to support researchers’ needs and provide support services to assist meeting researchers’ daily laboratory operations. The Genomics Core provides the following services:

  • Project planning support for researchers designing NGS experiments including assistance with data management support and new method development.
  • Serves as a catalyst for interaction and coordination with other genomics research resources at KU Lawrence (KULC) and regional institutions to build a strong foundation for genomics research throughout the University of Kansas institutions.
  • NGS sequencing using the Illumina NovaSeq X Plus high throughput sequencer.
  • 10x Genomics Chromium X single cell GEM-X 3’ expression, single cell 5’ expression v2, immune profiling (human or mouse / B-cell or T-cell), single cell ATAC v2, single cell multiome ATAC v2 + 3’ gene expression, and Chromium Fixed RNA – human or mouse transcriptome.
  • 10x Genomics Visium HD spatial expression – human or mouse transcriptome.
  • Mission Bio Tapestri single cell DNA interrogation.
  • Global sequence library preparation services and automated library preparation services.
  • Agilent TapeStation 4200 and Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 QC of RNA, DNA and sequence libraries.
  • RNA and genomic DNA isolation support services.
►
Histology | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Dianne Durham

The Histology Services facility houses sample preparation areas, including a fume hood and equipment for sample preparation for light and electron microscopy. The facility is supervised by a histology specialist who is responsible for maintaining all equipment and for training investigators and personnel in equipment use. The Histology laboratory is fully equipped for paraffin histology, including automated processing, embedding, sectioning, and staining. Facilities also are available for embedding and sectioning frozen specimens. For viewing sectioned material, the histology laboratory is equipped with dissecting and light microscopes.

The histology laboratory is housed in Hemenway Life Sciences Innovation Center (HLSIC) room 2037. Facilities for tissue preparation, embedding, sectioning, immunostaining, histochemistry, in situ PCR, and other procedures are housed in this space. Common-use procedure rooms equipped with peristaltic pumps for systemic perfusion of animals are located on the ground floor HLSIC vivarium as well as in a shared surgery suite adjacent to the Integrative Imaging Core. Complete facilities for tissue processing include equipment for solution preparation (pH meters, pipettors, hotplates, balances, mixing apparatus, ovens, and fume hoods for toxic substances). For paraffin sectioning, the facility possesses a new Leica ASP6025 S and a Leica ASP300S automated tissue processor, 2 Leica HistoCore Arcadia H & C Embedding Stations, and 2 fully automated Leica RM2255 microtomes, plus a manual Leica RM2235 microtome with associated water baths and slide drying plates. A Revco ultra-low freezer is used for tissue storage, and two well-performed cryostats – Thermo Scientific NX50 Cryostar, and Leica CM1950 are present for frozen sectioning. A Leica VT1000 S vibratome is available for thick sections. Sections are stained for light microscopy using a wide variety of conventional protocols with a Leica ST5020 automated slide stainer. A Leica 5030 robotic coverslipper and Primera EVO slide printer also facilitate slide processing. Tabletop microscopes are available in the laboratory to assess tissue quality during sectioning and staining.

►
Hoglund Biomedical Imaging Center (HBIC) | v2025.09 | Point(s) of Contact: Laura Martin, Swati Levendovszky

Established in 2003, the HBIC has greatly enhanced the KU research landscape. Top scientific researchers, renowned professors, graduate students and postdoctoral students aspire to carry out their work at HBIC, where advanced imaging studies have led to discoveries in major areas of research, including Alzheimer's disease, weight loss, fetal and infant health, multiple sclerosis, diabetes and brain injuries. HBIC provides outstanding imaging capabilities to complement the existing biomedical research community, including magnetic resonance imaging, magnetoencephalolgraphy, electroencephalography, magnetocardiography, and ultrasound.

►
Magnetic Resonance Imaging

A 3-Tesla Siemens Skyra human MRI scanner funded through an NIH High End Instrumentation grant (S10 RR29577) provides a full array of imaging capabilities including a variety of clinical MRI and MRS protocols, various head and body receive coils including a 32-channel head coil array, magnetic resonance elastrography. The Skyra is also equipped with a the multinuclear transmit/receive package and RF coils to allow non-proton acquisitions, including 19Fluorine and 129Xenon. The scanner is equipped with a FIRMM system (Framewise Integrated Real-time MRI Monitoring; Nous Imaging) to minimize head movement. The scanner is networked to our XNAT server to provide storage and seamless transfer of data to principal investigators and their research staff.

  • 129Xenon-MRI- A Polarean Xenon Mk-III polarizer is in 200 ft2 of laboratory space across the hall from the Skyra scanner. The polarizer produces 1-liter volumes of 129Xe polarized to >20% in one hour. Smaller volumes can be produced with polarization exceeding 30%.
  • Patient Monitoring & Physiological Recording- An MRI-compatible system (BIOPAC MP150 Data Acquisition and AcqKnowledge software) is used for recording physiological signals including respiration, pulse, and electrodermal activity for input into functional imaging analyses. MRI compatible EMG is also available (BrainVision). Additionally, an MRI compatible pulse oximetry, blood pressure monitoring, and EKG recording system (InVivoMetrics) is synchronized with the scanner to facilitate physiological gating of acquisitions. Analysis of heart rate variability is available using Kubios software.
  • Experimental Presentation- Experimental presentation and collection software is available on a workstation interfaced to the scanner: E-Prime 2.0 (Psychology Software Tools, Inc., Sharpsburg, PA), Presentation (Neurobehavioral Systems, Inc., Berkeley, CA)
  • Analysis Software- Data analysis support includes analysis computers running neuroimaging software (AFNI, Freesurfer, FSL, Matlab, SPM, LCModel), data analysis pipelines, data analysis quality checking through Redcap surveys, and data management tools (XNAT).
►
High Density Electroencephalography

The Magstim EGI GES 400 (Magstim EGI) system provides 128-channel infant/child EEG or 256-channel adult EEG. Geodesic EEG electrodes are evenly spaced over the entire scalp, cheeks and back of the neck, allowing for dense, even, high spatial resolution sampling. The system includes infant and adult sensor nets that allow for longitudinal studies. Other physiological measurements including respiratory flow, body position, blood oxygen saturation level (SpO2), EMG, and EKG that can be measured simultaneously with EEG. This system also interfaces with E-prime and Presentation software for evoked and event-related potentials. The system includes Net Station software that provides full acquisition, review, and analysis functions with GeoSource source estimation software. The scanner is networked to the KUMC shared network drives to provide seamless transfer of data to principal investigators and their research staff for analysis.

►
Clinical Space

Clinical space in the HBIC includes a patient waiting area, consultation room, changing suite, blood draw room, and cognitive testing room. Procedures available include physical examinations, neurological examinations, and blood draws, and height and weight measurements. Equipment includes a phlebotomy chair. Nursing support is provided by the Frontiers Clinical & Translational Science Unit. A neuropsychological testing room is located adjacent to the blood draw room and scanning facilities, equipped with paper and computer-based testing capabilities.

►
Image Analysis & Computing Laboratory

MRI data are transferred to and stored on a network server running XNAT (Extensible Neuroimaging Archive Toolkit) developed by Randy Buckner at Harvard University and the Neuroinformatics Research Group at Washington University School of Medicine), an open-source imaging informatics platform managed by KUMC Information Resources. Investigators can a Siemens Syngo workstation for offline analysis and exploring MRI data.

Our network-based analysis server (HBIC-SYNAPSE) has a large number of neuroimaging software packages installed. This resource is accessible by all Center users, and well-documented on our SharePoint site. HBIC Senior Scientists and Information Resources Department jointly manage this resource. Software includes E-Prime, Presentation, LabView, AFNI, BrainVoyager, SPM, FSL, LCModel, SPSS, SAS, Statistica, Matlab, IDL, GraphPad, Deltagraph, EndNote, Excel, Powerpoint, and Word. Data analysis support includes access to analysis server, data analysis protocol, data analysis quality checking through Redcap surveys, and data management tools (XNAT). The Image Analysis Laboratory also provides a suite of analysis pipelines for functional and structural imaging. These include validated methods for brain volume measurement, lesion quantification, arterial spin labeling quantification, fat/muscle analysis, kidney volume measurements, and functional analysis.

Analysis Software- EEGLab is used to analyze data. This software facilitates post-processing (filtering, averaging, artifact removal) of data, reconstruction of time-averaged data sets and cortical activity maps, and co-registering with EEG and MRI scans.

All HBIC computing resources are connected to the campus 10 Gigabit Ethernet core network and network file storage. Networked file servers provide constant hardware backups of stored data through mirrored storage systems and daily tape backups are also performed. Weekly tape backups are stored off site for additional protection of research data. The computers and network are managed by KUMC's Information Resources who provide installation, training, and maintenance on all information systems. The local area network is connected to a switched, 1 Gigabit Ethernet backbone that provides high speed Internet access through the KUMC Internet-2 communication network. The KU Medical Center’s centrally managed Data Centers house the infrastructure for our 450+ physical and virtual servers. The data centers also house a 1 Petabyte NAS for researchers to back up their primary research-related data.

The University of Kansas Medical Center is a member of the Kansas Research and Education Network (KanREN, Inc.) which provides us access to the commodity Internet (Internet 1), Internet 2 via the Great Plains Network (GPN), and connectivity to other Kansas educational/research institutions and Hospitals. The KanREN network was used to create a peering network between the University of Kansas, University of Kansas Medical Center, and the School of Medicine-Wichita. Setting up the peering network is the first step in providing seamless access to systems used by faculty, staff, students, and researchers spanning the campuses including the Advanced Computing Facility (ACF) located at the KU campus.

►
Integrative Imaging Core | v2025.02 | Point(s) of Contact: Dianne Durham

The Integrative Imaging Core Facility at the University of Kansas Medical Center provides training, access, and support on histology and imaging equipment for KUMC researchers at subsidized rates.

The imaging facility equipment includes an array of widefield and confocal fluorescent microscopes. The widefield systems include a Zeiss Axio Observer 7 system with AI Sample finder and Apotome optical sectioning, a Nikon High Content automated imaging system, a Nikon 90i motorized fluorescent microscope, Leica MZFLII and Nikon SMZ-1500 fluorescent stereomicroscopes, two Nikon 80i fluorescent microscopes, and an Olympus IX71 inverted fluorescent microscope. The imaging facility also has 3 confocal microscopes, including a Nikon A1R confocal, Leica SP8/STED 3x super resolution confocal microscope, and a Nikon CSU-W1 spinning-disk confocal microscope with SoRa super-resolution. In addition, the imaging core has dedicated image analysis workstations that includes software with 2D and 3D image analysis and deconvolution.

Spatial transcriptomics platforms offered by 10x Genomics are supported by the Integrative Imaging Core, including the 10x Visium (CytAssist) and Xenium solutions. Histology and Imaging core staff offer fee for service processing of tissue samples. Visium is offered through a collaboration between KUMC Integrative Imaging, Genomics, and Bioinformatics cores. The imaging facility houses, maintains, and operates the 10x CytAssist, an instrument that simplifies sample preparation and transfers the tissue of interest to a Visium capture area and the 10x Xenium Analyzer, an in-situ imaging system that maps gene targets in their spatial context with subcellular resolution. The core also stocks all equipment and non-10x branded reagents needed to complete associated protocols, reducing the entry burden for individual investigators to complete these experiments. The Genomics core is located a short walk away within the same building for easy handoff of Visium samples for sequencing. Bioinformatics core staff collaborate for high quality analysis and interpretation of the data output.

►
Laboratory Animal Resources | v2025.01 | Point(s) of Contact: Travis Hagedorn

The KUMC animal resources are comprised of 99,388 gross assigned ft² in four buildings located on the KUMC campus. The entire centralized animal care program at KUMC was fully accredited by the Association for Accreditation and Assessment of Laboratory Animal Care International (AAALAC) in February 1992 and has maintained its accreditation since that time. Suitable housing facilities are available for a wide variety of animal species, including the usual laboratory animals, as well as non-human primates. The facilities include a variety of dual-purpose animal rooms. Animals are housed separately by species and, when possible, by source and or microbiological status. The principal site is the Research Support Facility (RSF). The second animal facility occupies the fifth floor of the Smith Building, including support space as well as conventional rooms for housing rodent species, and large animals. A third animal facility is on the ground floor of the Hemenway Life Science Innovation Center. This facility includes rodent rooms and support space, including procedure rooms, the transgenic core facility, a rodent behavioral core, and an ABSL3 laboratory. The fourth site is a single animal room with one small surgical room, on the ground floor of the Hoglund Biomedical Imaging Center. LAR at KUMC is administratively responsible for all animal care resources and the purchase and care of all animals. LAR activities are overseen by Director of Veterinary Services/Attending Veterinarian Travis Hagedorn, DVM and Director of Operations Allison Neely, DVM, who are responsible for administrative, veterinary, and animal care staff. The Directors manage two full time clinical veterinarians and three veterinary technicians who provide veterinary support of animal research. This includes aspects of clinical care, technical assistance, interaction with the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee, protocol pre-review, and training of investigators. All veterinary functions are integrated with its consultative role, training requirement, and AALAS certification program. Many of the LAR animal technicians are certified by the American Association for Laboratory Animal Science, up to the highest level, Laboratory Animal Technologist. Special services provided by the LAR include the center for microimaging, surgery facilities, post-surgical care, radiology including x-ray and ultrasound, necropsies, and a wide variety of technical services.

►
Mass Spectrometry/Proteomics Core Laboratory | v2023.07 | Point(s) of Contact: Michael Washburn, Michaella Rekowski

The Mass Spectrometry and Proteomics Core Facility is located in Hemenway Research Building Room 1058. The MSP Core facility has been upgraded with high end mass spectrometers and sample preparation tools to support the various research interests on the KU Medical Center campus.

The facility is fully equipped with standard sample preparation equipment including sonicating water baths, thermomixers, balances, benchtop and tabletop centrifuges with adapters for multiple vessel types, a vacuum centrifuge and multiple refrigerators and freezers. The lab also has a biological safety cabinet and a fume hood. The instruments and equipment below are used to support the research interest of the KU Medical Center community through label-free or multiplexed (tandem mass tagged, TMT) proteomics, identification of post-translational modifications, cross-linked protein analysis, metabolomics and lipidomic analyses:

  • Thermo Orbitrap Fusion Lumos installed 05/2017 equipped with a Vanquish Neo UPLC interfaced to the mass spectrometer through a nano electrospray source.
  • Thermo Orbitrap Ascend installed 03/2023 equipped with a Vanquish Neo UPLC interfaced to the mass spectrometer through a nano electrospray source. This instrument is also equipped with high field asymmetric ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS Pro Duo) interface to remove interferants and improve sensitivity as well as real time searching (RTS) for multiplexed proteomics samples.
  • Bruker timsTOF HT installed 06/2023 equipped with a nanoElute 2 for proteomic applications using DIA-PASEF real time searching or Elute UPLC for metabolomic and lipidomic applications.
  • Multiple stand-alone data analysis workstations with dedicated software supporting multiple data analysis platforms
  • Vanquish Flex UPLC with UV detection for off-line separation and fractionation
  • PreOmics BeatBox for tissue homogenization and cell lysis
  • PreOmics PreON sample preparation robot to improve sample preparation throughout

Additionally, the MSP Core Facility staff is experienced in method development, application and data analysis to answer new or challenging biological questions.

►
Medicinal Chemistry Lab | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Raul Neri-Sierra, Obdulia Covarrubias-Zambrano, Divya Kamath, Stefan Bossmann

The Medicinal Chemistry Lab is a shared resource available to The University of Kansas Cancer Center members as well as external academic investigators and industry partners to establish collaborations. Services include research and development focused on the identification of preclinical candidates through synthesis chemistry, chemical biology, and emerging small-molecule therapeutic modalities.

The MedChem Lab aims to:

  • Provide expertise in medicinal chemistry and drug delivery in an integrated manner based on specific project activities;
  • Provide expertise in DNA/RNA vectors and advanced protein synthesis;
  • Provide seamless consulting at a substantially reduced cost in the discovery and development of novel therapeutics;
  • Provide expanded access to synthesis laboratory; and,
  • Offer or improve drug delivery services.

Preclinical Imaging Shared Resource (PISR) | v2025.03 | Point(s) of Contact: Stefan Bossmann

The Preclinical Imaging Core is a shared resource available to members of The University of Kansas Cancer Center, as well as scientists at other research and industry institutions. This shared resource provides access to top-of-the-line multimodal imaging modalities including optical (bioluminescence and fluorescence) tomography, photoacoustic and fluorescence tomography (PAFT), microComputed tomography (microCT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

The Preclinical Imaging Core is maintained with the materials necessary to operate each instrument, including a biological cabinet, anesthesia equipment and consumables such as oxygen, isoflurane and cleaning supplies which are regularly checked, re-stocked, calibrated, and maintained to ensure optimal functionality and availability.

Preclinical Imaging Core personnel are available to provide training for users to operate the equipment independently (IVIS) and assist in imaging when needed (IVIS, microCT, TriTom, and MRI). This model allows for streamlined scheduling of various projects while offering support for users requiring additional guidance during their studies.

IVIS

The Preclinical Imaging Core houses two IVIS Spectrums allowing for consistent access to both conventional and sterile housed animals. The IVIS Spectrum is capable of 2D and 3D optical tomography, with resolutions up to 20 microns. Fluorescence imaging can be performed in either reflectance or transillumination mode with a wide range of excitation and emission filters to accommodate a variety of targets. The newest manifold for the IVIS Spectrum can image up to 10 mice at a time allowing for streamlined data collection.

A Mouse Imaging Shuttle (MIS) is available for co-registration between microCT and 3D- bioluminescence and fluorescence images collected on the IVIS Spectrum providing the ability to seamlessly combine the capabilities of the two instruments.

microComputed Tomography

The Quantum GX2 microCT, provides access to high-speed, low dose computed tomography. The instrument is equipped with changeable x-ray filters, variable bore sizes, and allows reconstruction in matrices of 512 x 512 or 1024 x 1024 in each of the available fields of view (18, 36, 72, and 86 mm). Due to the modular bores and sample beds, subjects ranging in size from zebra fish to rabbits are easily accommodated. Should smaller volumes at higher image resolutions be necessary, the instrument provides the capacity for secondary sub-volume reconstruction without the need for additional acquisitions. Image resolutions up to 2.3-micron are possible with the use of sub-volume reconstruction techniques for ex-vivo samples.

Flexible imaging parameters facilitate in vivo imaging with available retrospective cardiac/respiratory gating, which can be applied to minimize motion artifacts, high-speed imaging, enabling image volume capture in as little as 3.9 seconds and “stitching” to cover large volumes of interest through a movable sample bed within the gantry to collect segments of data later combined into one continuous volume.

A Mouse Imaging Shuttle (MIS) is available for co-registration between microCT images and IVIS Spectrum bioluminescence and fluorescence images to combine the capabilities between the two instruments.

Photoacoustic and Fluorescense Tomography

The TriTom photoacoustic and fluorescence imaging platform enables researchers to conduct 3D- photoacoustic imaging with simultaneous fluorescence capabilities through a tunable laser. Within this platform, imaging resolutions of up to 160 x 470 microns in the sagittal plane and 160 x 160 microns in the transverse planes are achievable, allowing for detailed examination of anatomical, functional, and molecular processes. In vivo imaging occurs in a temperature-controlled chamber, and scan times can be completed in as little as 36 seconds. For contrast agent development, the cuvette sample holder can accommodate up to 10 contrast agents simultaneously, facilitating rapid testing across various wavelengths.

Magnetic Resonance Imaging

The 9.4 T Bruker MRI has a 30 cm bore to accommodate a broad range of sample sizes. This ultra-high-field instrument accommodates high-speed, high-resolution imaging with access to an extensive series of validated and pre-optimized protocols through Paravision360. Equipped with compatible small animal monitoring systems, a comprehensive range of surface and volumetric coils, parallel imaging upgrades, and multi-nuclear imaging channels, this instrument can be used to address a wide range of studies.

The Preclinical Imaging Core is available to support experimental planning and study design in anticipation of the arrival of this advanced MRI system.
